The American Express® Business Gold Card is one of the most rewarding business cards if you’re looking to earn Amex Membership Rewards points.

We’re currently seeing an excellent Amex Business Gold Card welcome offer, which is the biggest bonus we’ve ever seen on the card, making it the ideal time to apply. If you’re eligible for this card and the highest possible bonus, it’s absolutely worth taking advantage of, in my opinion.

Link: Learn more about the American Express® Business Gold Card

The Amex Business Gold Card currently has a massive welcome offer that’s as high as 200,000 Membership Rewards points after spending $15,000 on eligible purchases within the first three months. Welcome offers vary and you may not be eligible for an offer. Find out your offer.

Amex uses a variety of factors when it comes to deciding what offer people are eligible for, including history of opening and closing cards with Amex, spending history with Amex, how many welcome offers people have earned, etc. So, how does this Amex Business Gold Card bonus actually work?

You should find the highest possible offer through the above link. However, if you don’t, it can always be worth checking refer-a-friend links, opting in to targeted emails from Amex, or even using the CardMatch tool to see what you’re eligible for there. That being said, don’t expect to get a higher offer through any of those sources, since offers are typically targeted based on the person, rather than the application method.

It goes without saying that the Amex Business Gold bonus spending requirement is potentially significant, as it averages out to $5,000 per month. However, there are lots of ways to be creative with reaching minimum spending, and to make a plan. You could time your application around some large upcoming business expenses (whether that’s an ad campaign or buying inventory), prepay for some items, and maybe even put some expenses on credit cards that you might otherwise pay for with cash. #6142. Midterm Mayhem for the Free and Virtuous Society

The GOP will continue to suffer at the polls until it focuses on building this type of society once again.

President Donald Trump speaks in front of a portrait of Ronald Reagan at the White House in Washington, D.C., March 24, 2026.

There has been some pretty unsurprising but bad analysis of the election results since Tuesday night. There also has been some very good analysis, from National Review’s editors, from our own Jim Geraghty, from our own Dan McLaughlin, from Yuval Levin, from Erick Erickson, and plenty of others on the conservative right. There is no need for a redundant analysis that merely restates what has already been said, even though an amen to all of what they said should be assumed. What I want to suggest, in total alignment with my aforementioned friends and colleagues, is that these election results capture the very essence of the twin deficits in the Trump-era moment: a newfound contempt for both the free and the virtuous society.

The debate over the Iran war’s role in this Republican debacle would be comical if it were not so maddening. With virtually no one operating in good faith or making a serious argument, a whole cabal of people have claimed, all statistical evidence and voter polling to the contrary, that the sole reason for states like Texas, Kansas, and Mississippi flipping is the Iran war. Inversely, no one who disputes that monocausal theory of the case denies that the Iran war is unpopular, and that its unpopularity was a contributor to the decline of approval for President Trump and to the results Republicans suffered all over the country Tuesday night. That voters detest the state of prices, and that they believe (with obvious basis in fact) that tariffs are connected to this, is not disputable by credible people. That the bizarre handling of the Iran war led to a Strait of Hormuz debacle, and to significant problems for fuel prices and a downstream impact from diesel prices, is also obvious. Reasonable people can disagree as to how much of the Iran war contribution was related to opposition to de-nuclearizing Iran versus the way in which it all went (e.g., a failed MOU negotiated by the vice president, repeated claims of victory that were obviously untrue, and a sustained period of time with no clear resolution). But all advocates of a multi-causal explanation of the midterms recognize the significant role Iran played.

#6140. Elizabeth Warren May Team Up With Trump On A 10% Credit Card Interest Cap—Putting Your Credit And Rewards At Risk

Both Elizabeth Warren and President Trump want to cap credit card interest rates, even as AI pushes long-term interest rates higher. And Warren is making a full court press to work with the President to make this happen. Donald Trump and J.D. Vance, and Elizabeth Warren and Bernie Sanders, actually agree on a lot of economics. They share the same distrust of markets, dislike of market outcomes, and generally lean into the same government interventions. “Horseshoe theory” suggests the political spectrum bends into a U, with supposedly opposing ends becoming closer to each other than their labels would suggest. National conservatives and progressive populists both argue that powerful interests have rigged the economy, that international competition has harmed American workers, and that government should dictate outcomes. Their constituencies are different and who they want to benefit are different but their economics are often the same. Here’s Warren saying she wants to work with the President on their shared goals. Sen. Elizabeth Warren (D-MA) says she wants to work with President Trump to cap credit card interest rates at 10% and Democrats “have the bills ready to go” to work with the president. “We got a whole bunch more that the American people have told us that they want on price gouging, on protecting our rural hospitals, on making sure people have access to healthcare,” she says. “…We got a lot of ways to deliver for the American people, whether Donald Trump wants to be a part of it or not.” — Face The Nation (@FaceTheNation) November 8, 2026 The economic illiteracy here is downright dangerous. Limits credit availability. Unsecured credit is expensive for a reason. Default risk, fraud, and card servicing mean that rates actually need to be higher to offer the product to most people. You’ll have fewer credit applications approved, reduced credit lines, and closed accounts – focusing on the riskiest borrowers. It’s only better-credit borrowers who might still get credit. Forces people into worse products. The need for credit doesn’t go away, just the best options people have been choosing for credit. So they get pushed into payday loans, overdrawing checking accounts, pawn shops, etc. Drives up card fees. If issuers can’t charge current rates, they have to generate revenue in fees – annual fees, balance transfer fees, etc. Bad for the economy. Unsecured credit makes transactions easy and frictionless. Less credit means fewer transactions, less economy activity. Destroys rewards programs. When products aren’t profitable there’s little reason to incentivize transactions. Better rewards cards often rebate the full value of merchant swipe fees to the consumer, spending on rewards in search of consumers who will revolve balances. When that’s not profitable anymore, the card programs no longer make sense. And that also hurts airlines, makes flights less profitable, and there’ll be fewer flights and at higher cost. Increases market concentration. Thin-margin card issuers and smaller players get pushed out, while larger issuers can cross-sell products and operate more efficiently surviving longer. Credit cards are a very competitive space (and if they could make money at 10% APR, they’d do it to win business). But this competition will erode under an APR cap. Hurts credit scores. As credit limits get cut, credit utilization spikes which drives down credit scores. That also makes other borrowing (auto, mortgage, even insurance pricing in some states) more expensive. In the most simplistic thinking, ‘stuff is unaffordable’ so we’ll ‘pass a law that says it should be more affordable.’ But that’s not how policy works. You don’t get to dictate outcomes, just the rules of the game, and that leads to outcomes including unintended consequences. Here, it’s almost as though those outcomes are intended because they’re so obvious. Donald Trump and J.D. Vance, and Elizabeth Warren and Bernie Sanders, actually agree on a lot of economics. They share the same distrust of markets, dislike of market outcomes, and generally lean into the same government interventions.

“Horseshoe theory” suggests the political spectrum bends into a U, with supposedly opposing ends becoming closer to each other than their labels would suggest. National conservatives and progressive populists both argue that powerful interests have rigged the economy, that international competition has harmed American workers, and that government should dictate outcomes. Their constituencies are different and who they want to benefit are different but their economics are often the same.

Here’s Warren saying she wants to work with the President on their shared goals.

Sen. Elizabeth Warren (D-MA) says she wants to work with President Trump to cap credit card interest rates at 10% and Democrats “have the bills ready to go” to work with the president.

“We got a whole bunch more that the American people have told us that they want on price gouging, on protecting our rural hospitals, on making sure people have access to healthcare,” she says. “…We got a lot of ways to deliver for the American people, whether Donald Trump wants to be a part of it or not.”

— Face The Nation (@FaceTheNation) November 8, 2026

The economic illiteracy here is downright dangerous.

Limits credit availability. Unsecured credit is expensive for a reason. Default risk, fraud, and card servicing mean that rates actually need to be higher to offer the product to most people. You’ll have fewer credit applications approved, reduced credit lines, and closed accounts – focusing on the riskiest borrowers. It’s only better-credit borrowers who might still get credit.

Forces people into worse products. The need for credit doesn’t go away, just the best options people have been choosing for credit. So they get pushed into payday loans, overdrawing checking accounts, pawn shops, etc.

Drives up card fees. If issuers can’t charge current rates, they have to generate revenue in fees – annual fees, balance transfer fees, etc.

Bad for the economy. Unsecured credit makes transactions easy and frictionless. Less credit means fewer transactions, less economy activity.

Destroys rewards programs. When products aren’t profitable there’s little reason to incentivize transactions. Better rewards cards often rebate the full value of merchant swipe fees to the consumer, spending on rewards in search of consumers who will revolve balances. When that’s not profitable anymore, the card programs no longer make sense. And that also hurts airlines, makes flights less profitable, and there’ll be fewer flights and at higher cost.

Increases market concentration. Thin-margin card issuers and smaller players get pushed out, while larger issuers can cross-sell products and operate more efficiently surviving longer. Credit cards are a very competitive space (and if they could make money at 10% APR, they’d do it to win business). But this competition will erode under an APR cap.

Hurts credit scores. As credit limits get cut, credit utilization spikes which drives down credit scores. That also makes other borrowing (auto, mortgage, even insurance pricing in some states) more expensive. In the most simplistic thinking, ‘stuff is unaffordable’ so we’ll ‘pass a law that says it should be more affordable.’ But that’s not how policy works. You don’t get to dictate outcomes, just the rules of the game, and that leads to outcomes including unintended consequences. Here, it’s almost as though those outcomes are intended because they’re so obvious. #6139. Aer Lingus Pilots Threatened With Criminal Charges Over Bomb Threat Diversion

Last week, I covered how dozens of flights across Europe were faced with bomb threats. It was clearly a hoax, but these have to be taken seriously, and we saw all kinds of diversions, flight cancelations, and more.

Europe’s largest union representing pilots is now sharing the details of an incident that happened with one of these diversions, whereby an Aer Lingus flight was forced by fighter jets to divert to a French military base. When the pilots weren’t comfortable doing so, they were reportedly threatened with criminal charges.

This incident happened on Thursday, November 5, 2026, and involves Aer Lingus flight EI402, scheduled to operate from Dublin (DUB) to Rome (FCO). The Airbus A320 with the registration code EI-DEH took off at 6:40AM local time, and made its way southeast toward Rome.

The A320 flew for around an hour, and made it just past Paris, when the plane changed heading and prepared to divert. French fighter jets had been deployed to escort the aircraft, and demanded that it divert to a French military base. Specifically, the plane diverted to Évreux-Fauville Air Base (EVX), located in Normandy.

The plane touched down there at 10:05AM local time, 2hr25min after it first departed (there was a one hour time change). Coincidentally, that’s basically the same flight time as it would’ve been to Rome, as the aircraft had to hold for an extended period of time.

The plane ended up returning to Dublin later in the day, departing at 4:59PM local time, and landing in Dublin at 5:20PM local time, after a flight time of 1hr21min. So passengers spent nearly 12 hours on the plane, only to end up back where they started. Man, that’s rough, especially when you consider these A320s don’t have power ports, Wi-Fi, etc.

Here’s where the story gets really interesting, as explained by the European Cockpit Association (ECA), which represents over 44,000 pilots across Europe, including pilots at Aer Lingus. The union is expressing serious concerns about how this incident was handled.

What happened is that the Aer Lingus pilots didn’t want to divert to Évreux-Fauville Air Base, because they didn’t have the necessary operational information and aeronautical charts to land there. They requested a landing at another airport, but were rejected. According to the pilots, they were even threatened with criminal charges if they didn’t divert to the airport as requested.

That’s the point on which the union is sounding the alarm. Let me just quote the union on this:

As representatives of the pilot profession, ECA, IALPA and SNPL fully recognise and appreciate the assistance provided by authorities in responding to these threats and supporting flight crews in bringing their passengers and aircraft to safety.

However, reports indicate that, in certain circumstances, military aircraft have intercepted civilian airliners and directed aircraft commanders to land at specific airports without adequately considering aircrafts’ operational and safety requirements.

According to information received by IALPA, in one recent incident involving an Aer Lingus aircraft, military fighter aircraft directed the flight crew to divert to a military airfield for which they did not have the necessary aeronautical charts and operational information to safely conduct a landing. Despite the flight crew seeking an alternative and more suitable diversion airport, their request was refused.

ECA, IALPA and SNPL are also alarmed by subsequent reports that the pilots were apparently faced by the prospect of possible criminal prosecution for actions that were, at all times, aimed at protecting their passengers, crew and aircraft.

The union emphasizes that the captain of a flight should have the ultimate responsibility for the safety of passengers, crew, and the aircraft, and that the captain is uniquely positioned to assess the operational circumstances and determine the safest course of action, taking account of all relevant factors, including aircraft performance, available aeronautical information, airport suitability, operational limitations, and the availability of emergency assistance on the ground.

The union points out how the prospect of criminal prosecution against pilots exercising their professional judgment in such circumstances risks undermining aviation safety, and the effective cooperation between flight crews and authorities.

An Aer Lingus A320 was recently forced to divert to a military base in France, after the aircraft faced a bomb threat (which also impacted dozens of other flights). Fighter jets reportedly demanded the plane divert to this airport despite objections from the pilots, who felt they didn’t have sufficient operational information and aeronautical charts to land there.

The union representing pilots claims that the pilots were threatened with criminal charges if they didn’t divert there, which the union believes undermines the responsibility that pilots should have over the safety of their aircraft.

I fully side with the pilots and union here. It’s silly to me that a bomb threat that’s an obvious hoax puts pilots in a situation where they don’t feel comfortable landing at, with no alternatives offered.

What do you make of this Aer Lingus pilot situation?

These hoaxes (almost certainly organized by Russia) have a higher probability of real negative consequences (accidents, deaths) if European authorities over-react in a panicked, thoughtless fashion. Especially for low credibility threats (not clear that we should divert these flights at all), but reasonable operational considerations should be made such as just choosing a new route with minimal city overflight to a facility where the aircraft can be quickly screened then continue to its destination in a manner the airline finds to balance various operational considerations.

While I appreciate the concern of the pilots here, ultimately, if you have a serious threat, landing at a commercial airport is the absolute last thing you want to do. It's not about inconvenience at that point, it's about safety. If the threat was real, yeah, sorry, I don't want that plane landing at CDG just because it's expedient. Get it to a more controlled place. Deal with the threat. And Ben, you're take on WiFi and power outlets is really a poor one. It could have been an A380, or an ERJ, ATR, or anything in between. Keeping some phones charged is really low on the priority list.

"I fully side with the pilots and union here."

Realizing that fighter pilots do not typically give out such instructions on interceptions, I checked and learned that they did not do so here. Fighter interceptor pilots are usually under the control of air defense controllers and on their frequency. It was the French civilian air traffic controllers issuing the instructions to Air Lingus on their air control frequency. Ex-fighter pilot.

#6138. End Of An Era: Hong Kong’s Iconic “Symphony Of Lights” Show Ending

Hong Kong is one of my favorite cities in the world. When I think of Hong Kong, the beautiful waterfront and skyline on both sides of Victoria Harbour come to mind. Along those lines, a nightly staple of the waterfront is coming to an end, and I’m sad about it…

Since 2004, Hong Kong has had the “Symphony of Lights” show every single night at 8PM, lasting for around 10 minutes. It holds the Guinness World Record for being the world’s largest permanent light and sound show, as it involves dozens of buildings.

It’s one of the things that contributes to Hong Kong’s electric energy, as you have a sea of people lining up on the waterfront (typically on the Tsim Sha Tsui side, though sometimes also on the Central side) every night to watch it.

Well, after 22 years, the Symphony of Lights will be coming to an end. The last show is expected to take place on Wednesday, November 18, 2026. To mark the end of the era, the final show will feature special pyrotechnics and fireworks.

Why has Hong Kong decided to end the nightly Symphony of Lights show? Officially, it’s a strategic shift in the city’s tourism and event strategy, described as being driven by shifting visitor habits, diminishing appeal, high maintenance costs, and a pivot to seasonal attractions. We’re told that we can expect “something new” in the future, but it doesn’t sound like it’ll be a full replacement for the Symphony of Lights.

I must admit, I’m sad to see this change in Hong Kong. No matter how often I visited Hong Kong, I always made a point of watching the Symphony of Lights, and always found it to be so enjoyable. Hong Kong has one of the world’s most gorgeous skylines, and the nightly show just took that to the next level.

I am curious what the backstory here is. Was the cost of operating this really so high, in the scheme of things? While I can in theory appreciate the concept of diminishing appeal, the nightly show always had a crowd in the thousands waiting to enjoy it — that was true 20 years ago when I first visited Hong Kong, and it was also true when I visited earlier this year.

Hong Kongers will soon have to bid farewell to the Symphony of Lights, the iconic nightly show that has been lighting up the city’s skyline since 2004. Officially, this change is described as being due to shifting visitor habits, diminishing appeal, high maintenance costs, and a pivot to seasonal attractions.

I’ve enjoyed this show every time I visited Hong Kong, so I’m sad to see this development. The skyline is still incredible and leaves me in awe every time, but there’s no denying that the nightly show added just a little bit of extra sparkle.

What do you make of Hong Kong’s nightly Symphony of Lights ending?

As iconic as it is, I understand why they don't feel the need to keep it in its current form. #6136. American Airlines Plans To Bring Back First Class Mini-Meals On Shorter Flights—Starting With New York–Chicago

This is a very good change. A flight can take up much of your afternoon without crossing American’s 900-mile meal threshold, especially when you include getting to the airport, boarding, and a connection. A small meal makes first class more worthwhile.

JonNYC reports that American Airlines is bringing back light bites and mini-meals on 700–899-mile domestic first class flights, starting on NYC/ORD.

American used to have a service between a basket of packaged snacks and a full meal. Before the pandemic, shorter flights could get something plated that would tide you over.

In 2016 I reported plans for plated morning items, including yogurt and breakfast cake. And my 2018 menu coverage included Lite Bites cheeses with cracked black pepper cheddar, cave-aged cheddar, Appalachian Tomme, and smoked Gouda.

American’s mainline standard is a snack basket on 500–899-mile flights during meal times, with meals starting in the 900-mile range.

United actually raised its meal threshold from 800 to 900 miles in January 2024. American would be moving in the other direction, offering something more substantial on flights where Delta and United generally hand out snacks.

Alaska is still the standard to beat. They already feed passengers on shorter flights, and I’ve found their domestic first class food better than competitors’.

New York–Chicago is an obvious place to start. New York LaGuardia–O’Hare is about 730 miles, and New York JFK–O’Hare about 740. An expansion might include:

American also used to have meal “exception markets”: shorter routes that got meals for competitive reasons. My January 2020 service guide listed Chicago–Dallas, Chicago–Boston, Chicago–New York, Los Angeles–Denver, and LaGuardia–Atlanta, among others.

I like a broad 700–899-mile rule better than making customers depend on whether their particular city pair merits an exception, though the exception markets got real meals and some were even shorter like Chicago–Washington National at just 612 miles which still wouldn’ qualify for a lite bite under this distance band.

This does mean more work for flight attendants. Individual food service means preparation, distribution, and clearing, with less time to do it on a shorter flight. American is also adding first class seats to some of its aircraft.

The airline’s product turnaround has been surprising, and surprisingly fast. They’ve introduced new business class suites, improved regional cabins and internet, upgraded coffee, and put money into lounges. They’re also reversing years of bad product decisions, including plans to bring back seatback screens and add more extra legroom coach seats.

Their returning coach food reservation program, announced with an initial Dallas–Fort Worth–Los Angeles test, should help passengers get the item they actually want. Mostly, though, I like that American seems to be loading enough food that there’s still something left when the cart reaches my aisle.

American has now announced the return of lite bites, with options including:

There will be two options onboard a given flight, with choices rotating “throughout the year.”

In my opinion, this is the type of change that AA needs to be doing. It’s one thing to match Delta and United but those airlines have already done what AA is matching so AA “premium” is looked at as “matching” vs finding ways to provide their own premium offering unique to AA (for now) where AA gets the credit for incrementally approving service levels across the industry, not just catching up.

This is what Delta was so good at in the 2010s. –Very small incremental improvements that really weren’t ever much (but marketed as being the best thing since the introduction of alcohol to airlines) but they were over and above competitors and they’d get “premium” credit for improving the customer experience even though Delta lagged (and still does in a number of areas) in “premium” vs competitors.

It’s the claiming your own “premium” narrative that AA needs to be focused on vs “catching up” in my opinion

@Drew Gary did a good article on that exact topic https://viewfromthewing.com/american-airlines-meal-rule-has-no-exceptions-except-one-route-tied-to-an-airport-that-closed-in-1995/

Now THIS is healthy competition… adding new amenities to stand out among its foes… good on you, American Airlines. I’ll say, was booked on WN for NYC-Chicago, but they failed me, and AA saved me, so… yeah… operational reliability matters, too, folks.

The press release actually contains items that look like real food. Not just a cheese plate (although I’m sure that will often be what’s available). Most importantly it shows AA understands it needs to compete in the main HNWI markets – NY, Chicago, LA. This is a very positive sign.

Lite Bites were also served on CLT-BOS, which is 727 miles. One of the few reasons I would intentionally connect at CLT pre-pandemic. This restoration is most welcomed.

And yes, there had better be warm nuts with these restored Lite Bites.

#6135. Hegseth Impeachment Vote Imminent

There is a significant chance that one or more articles will be approved.

Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth testifies about the Pentagon’s fiscal year 2027 budget request before the House Armed Services Committee in Washington, D.C., April 29, 2026.

Eight articles of impeachment against Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth have been proposed in the House by Representative Thomas Massie, a libertarian Republican from Kentucky who lost his seat when the president pushed for his ouster in a primary earlier this year. (The Trump-endorsed candidate, Ed Gallrein, retained the seat for the GOP last week despite the wave that will give Democrats solid majorities in both congressional chambers come January.)

Though still narrowly controlled by Republicans for the next two lame duck months, the House will be forced to consider Massie’s proposal. Impeachment is a privileged motion under House rules; action of some kind must be taken on it within two days after it is filed. Impeachments can stretch beyond a single session of Congress, so if the House impeaches Hegseth, a Senate trial could be postponed until January, when Democrats will have a commanding majority in the upper chamber.

#6134. Buy Wyndham Rewards Points With Best-Ever 100% Bonus (0.65 Cents Each): Worth It?

Wyndham Rewards has launched its latest promotion on purchased points, which is potentially in line with the best-ever offers that we’ve seen from the program. This could be a great value for unlocking discounted award stays, as the program is offering up to a 100% bonus, which is an opportunity to acquire points for 0.65 cents each.

Link: Buy Wyndham Rewards points with a bonus

Between 12:01AM ET on November 11 and 11:59PM on December 31, 2026, Wyndham Rewards is offering a bonus on purchased points. The best offer appears to be for up to a 100% bonus, though you’ll have to log into your account to see what you’re eligible for.

With this offer, you can unlock the highest bonus if you purchase at least 3,000 points in one transaction. If you purchase 1,000 or 2,000 points, you don’t receive any bonus. If you purchase points, they’ll post to your account within 72 hours, and purchases are non-refundable. Purchased points don’t count toward Wyndham Rewards elite status.

Ordinarily you can buy Wyndham Rewards points for 1.3 cents each, before any discounts or bonuses, and that includes all taxes and fees.

If you maxed out the promotion and were eligible for a 100% bonus, you could purchase 400,000 points (including 200,000 bonus points) for $2,600, which is a rate of 0.65 cents per point.

This is the best bonus offer I ever recall seeing from Wyndham Rewards, so if there has ever been a time to buy points, this is it.

Wyndham Rewards ordinarily lets members purchase up to 100,000 points per account per calendar year, before any bonuses. However, during this promotion, that cap has been doubled, to 200,000 points.

When Wyndham offers a promotion on purchased points, it’s most commonly an 80-100% bonus. So this 100% bonus is at the very top end of that scale. However, personally I’d decide on whether to make a purchase more based on if I had an immediate use in mind, rather than the exact cost per point.

Below is a chart with some of the recent promotions we saw from Wyndham Rewards on buying points, before this one, with the highest bonus amounts offered.

Wyndham Rewards points purchases are processed by points.com, meaning they don’t count as a hotel purchase for the purposes of credit card spending.

I’d recommend using a card with which you’re trying to reach a minimum spending requirement, or a credit card that maximizes your return on everyday spending. When in doubt, review which credit cards are best for buying points and miles.

Generally speaking, I only recommend buying points when you have a specific, short-term use in mind. In the case of Wyndham Rewards points:

More generally, there are definitely some properties where there’s value in outright buying points for the purposes of a redemption. Let me actually give a direct example, as I recently purchased some Wyndham points for a hotel stay, rather than booking with cash. I needed to be in Colorado Springs, and I booked The Mining Exchange Hotel, part of Wyndham Registry Collection (the hotel even has a Michelin key!)

The cash rate for a base room at the hotel would’ve been $307.57, inclusive of taxes & fees.

Meanwhile the hotel was charging just 30,000 points. At a rate of 0.65 cents per point, that’s like paying $195 for the stay, inclusive of taxes & fees. Not bad, eh?

Well, it gets better than that. Wyndham Rewards often lets you book premium rooms at no extra cost when redeeming points, so I was able to book a club room for the same 30,000 points.

If paying cash, that would’ve cost $438.54, inclusive of taxes & fees.

Now, the club rooms absolutely aren’t worth it, since you just get access to a pantry with some packaged snacks. But hey, if the cost is the same, I’ll take it. 😉

Wyndham Rewards has a four tier award chart, so free night redemptions will cost one of the following amounts:

While I wouldn’t say there’s widespread appeal to buying Wyndham Rewards points for these kinds of redemptions, there are some situations where the numbers will work out. Perhaps the best value would come in situations where you just need to buy a few thousand points to have enough for an award stay.

Wyndham Rewards has more than 9,000 hotels across 20 brands in 80+ countries. Some of the most popular Wyndham Rewards brands include Registry Collection, Wyndham Grand, Dolce, Wyndham, La Quinta, Wingate, Wyndham Garden, Ramada, Days Inn, Super 8, Howard Johnson, and Travelodge.

Everyone will value points differently. Based on my latest miles & points valuations, I consider Wyndham Rewards points to be worth 0.6 cents each. Admittedly that’s a very conservative valuation, and there should be opportunities to get way more value than that.

Wyndham Rewards has one of the most complicated points expiration policies of any hotel loyalty program:

Wyndham Rewards partners with a variety of transferable points currencies, including Bilt Rewards, Capital One, Chase Ultimate Rewards, and Citi ThankYou. The catch is that transfers are at a 1:1 ratio, so I wouldn’t at all consider that to be a good redemption value.

That’s because you could be getting way more value from your transferable points than moving them to a program where points can be purchased for well under a penny each.

Wyndham Rewards also has a portfolio of credit cards issued in the United States, which are potentially quite lucrative if you frequent the brand.

Wyndham Rewards is offering up to a 100% bonus on purchased points, which is an opportunity to buy points for as little as 0.65 cents each. While I most definitely wouldn’t speculatively buy Wyndham Rewards points at this cost, there are some situations where the math works out, so everyone should crunch the numbers for themselves.

To those who are Wyndham Rewards fans, are there any properties you can get outsized value at with this promotion?

#6133. United Airlines Plans Seatback Screens And Bigger Bins For Aging Boeing 757-300s—Retirement Can Wait

United Airlines is planning a major cabin upgrade for its 21 Boeing 757-300s, bringing seatback entertainment, larger overhead bins and refreshed interiors to planes that average roughly 24 years old. American Airlines retired its last 757s early in the pandemic. United apparently sees enough flying left in these stretched jets to spend money on them. According to aviation watchdog JonNYC, the work will bring the aircraft into the airline’s United Next cabin program. That’s a strong indication they’re sticking around for years, even as United replaces a different part of its 757 fleet with new Airbus aircraft. Jon reports that the 757-300 modification includes: Boeing Space Bins, providing more overhead storage. Panasonic on-demand entertainment at every seat. A full cabin in-seat power system. New cabin dividers, headers and United branding. Refreshed seats and cabin fixtures throughout the aircraft. JonNYC’s report on United’s Boeing 757-300 cabin upgrades — JonNYC (@xJonNYC), November 10, 2026 He says the delay involved getting larger bins certified for this particular version of the 757. Going through that work for the 21 airplanes is a substantial commitment. The current 757-300 cabin relies on entertainment streamed to your own device. The planes already have power. Screens and larger bins are big improvements. The Specific 757-300 Plan Is New United’s broad promise to upgrade its domestic cabins goes back to the original United Next announcement in June 2021. Back then, they said the retrofit would be 99% complete by summer 2025. That… didn’t happen. When United placed their huge 2021 aircraft order, Andrew Nocella said it wasn’t intended to replace the 757-300s. What’s been missing is a concrete upgrade plan for a small fleet that kept flying with a noticeably older product while hundreds of other aircraft received new interiors. Now we know the plan, and why it took so long. United’s Two 757 Fleets Have Different Futures The 757-300 is the long, high-capacity domestic aircraft. The shorter 757-200 is the one associated with United’s thin transatlantic routes and premium transcontinental flying. United Aircraft Fleet Current Seats Plan Boeing 757-300 21 234, including 24 domestic first class United Next cabin upgrade reported by JonNYC Boeing 757-200 40 176, including 16 lie-flat business class Replacement flying by Airbus A321XLRs and A321neo Coastliners United’s last annual report put the average age of the -300s at 23.3 years at the end of 2025, versus 28.9 years for the -200s. United also owns all 21 of the stretched planes. In March, United laid out that premium Airbus narrowbodies would replace the flying of 40 Boeing 757-200s. United’s first A321XLR entered domestic service in September. I’ve covered how the A321XLR changes the economics of those thinner international routes. United’s have 150 seats, including 20 business class and 12 premium economy seats. American accelerated its 757 retirement in 2020, eliminating an aircraft type and the associated training and maintenance costs. American never operated the -300. How The 757 Became So Hard To Replace The 757 entered service in 1983 as a more efficient replacement for the Boeing 727. It combined two engines, a two-pilot cockpit and a new wing with the ability to operate from demanding airports. Boeing developed it alongside the 767, with closely related cockpits allowing pilots to qualify on both. It became useful for far more than its original domestic role: busy trunk routes, transcontinental flights, Hawaii, leisure flying and eventually thinner routes across the Atlantic. The combination of payload, range and strong performance on shorter runways and at hot or high-altitude airports gave airlines options that weren’t available from smaller narrowbodies. Approvals for extended overwater flying helped open transatlantic routes. Continental used the 757-200 to connect Newark with European cities that couldn’t support a bigger airplane. Winter headwinds meant that United was said to operate focus cities at Goose Bay and Gander. But selling enough seats to support a 757 was easier than filling a widebody. The -300 entered service in 1999 with Condor, adding 23 feet, 4 inches of fuselage to carry more passengers, with less range than the -200. Only 55 were built. Continental took its first 757-300 in December 2001, initially deploying it on domestic routes from Newark. Familiar routes include Chicago–San Francisco, Chicago–Los Angeles and Washington Dulles–Los Angeles. It’s an unusually long airplane with just one aisle. United’s regular domestic A321neo carries 200 passengers. Its 757-300 carries 234, including four more first class seats. That’s 34 additional customers on one departure. An A321 can be configured much more densely, but United couldn’t simply swap in its current domestic Airbus cabin and preserve that capacity. The Airbus A321XLR comes closest to replacing the 757’s longer missions. And its advertised range of up to 4,700 nautical miles exceeds the 757’s. The missing airplane is one that combines all the desired capacity, runway performance, payload and operating economics. I recently wrote about Scott Kirby complaining that he’s been asking for a 757 replacement for more than 20 years. Boeing studied a new middle-of-the-market airplane, often called the “797,” but never launched it. Boeing ended 757 production in 2004 and delivered the last aircraft in 2005. United Next Is Still A Work In Progress The cabin program has made substantial progress since I covered the first Airbus retrofit in early 2023, but the original summer 2025 finish slipped badly. United reported more than 530 new and retrofitted aircraft with its signature interior at the end of 2025. In March 2026, they said 70% of the narrowbody retrofit plan was complete. The most recent broader measure is from last week: more than 181,000 seatback screens, covering about 85% of the mainline fleet. That includes aircraft with older entertainment systems, so it isn’t an 85% completion figure for United Next. On the October 21 earnings call, Nocella said United expects to finish installing its signature cabins, including screens, larger bins and new lighting, by the end of 2027. Starlink Is Coming To The 757s, But None Are Equipped Yet United’s official Starlink tracker, updated November 11, shows: 691 aircraft equipped: 352 regional jets, 332 mainline narrowbodies and seven widebodies. 54% of daily flights operating with Starlink. The tracker shows 46% completion of its aircraft installation program. All 61 Boeing 757s listed as “coming soon.” None is shown with Starlink installed. That includes the 21 757-300s. So they’re in the plan. I’ve covered United’s accelerated Starlink installation plans. Their latest targets are coverage of 61% of departures by the end of this year, 87% by June 1, 2027, and completion of the fleet rollout by the end of 2027. For now, a United 757 still means the older internet. United’s tracker lets you check a specific flight within three days of departure. According to aviation watchdog JonNYC, the work will bring the aircraft into the airline’s United Next cabin program. That’s a strong indication they’re sticking around for years, even as United replaces a different part of its 757 fleet with new Airbus aircraft.

Jon reports that the 757-300 modification includes:

JonNYC’s report on United’s Boeing 757-300 cabin upgrades — JonNYC (@xJonNYC), November 10, 2026

He says the delay involved getting larger bins certified for this particular version of the 757. Going through that work for the 21 airplanes is a substantial commitment.

The current 757-300 cabin relies on entertainment streamed to your own device. The planes already have power. Screens and larger bins are big improvements.

United’s broad promise to upgrade its domestic cabins goes back to the original United Next announcement in June 2021. Back then, they said the retrofit would be 99% complete by summer 2025. #6131. Buy IHG One Rewards Points With 100% Bonus (0.5 Cents Each): Worth It?

IHG One Rewards is currently offering a limited time 100% bonus on purchased points. With this, IHG One Rewards members can purchase points for as little as 0.5 cents each. Is this a good deal?

While I wouldn’t recommend buying points without a specific use in mind, there are absolutely ways to get outsized value, and this is in line with the best offers that we see from the program. With the right strategy, this could be an opportunity to get a significant discount on an IHG hotel stay, and I’ll show exactly how.

Link: Buy IHG One Rewards points with this promotion with a 100% bonus

Between 12:01AM ET on November 11 and 11:59PM ET on November 15, 2026, IHG One Rewards is offering a bonus on purchased points. Points can be purchased in increments of 1,000 points, and the bonus is structured as follows:

Note that the purchase of IHG points doesn’t count toward elite status, and purchased points will post within 72 hours of an eligible purchase (though usually much faster than that).

Ordinarily you can buy IHG One Rewards points for as little as one cent each (the pricing isn’t linear), before any discounts or bonuses, and that’s inclusive of all taxes and fees.

With that in mind, if you were eligible for a 100% bonus and purchased 200,000 IHG One Rewards points pre-bonus, you’d receive a total of 400,000 points at a cost of $2,000, which is a rate of 0.5 cents per IHG point.

While The Brand New IHG One Rewards Premier Select Credit Card (learn more), The New IHG One Rewards Premier Credit Card (learn more), The New IHG One Rewards Credit Card (learn more), and The New IHG One Rewards Business Credit Card (learn more), offer a 30% discount on purchased points, that benefit only applies when buying points at the normal cost, and wouldn’t be applicable here.

IHG One Rewards ordinarily lets members purchase up to 150,000 points per calendar year, before any bonuses. However, during this promotion that cap has been increased to 200,000 points, pre-bonus.

When IHG One Rewards does offer a promotion on purchased points, the 100% bonus or 50% discount is the most common offer. A 100% bonus and 50% discount give you the same price per point, so you’ll typically pay 0.5 cents per point during a promotion.

Below is a chart with some of the recent promotions we saw from the program, before this one.

IHG One Rewards points purchases are processed by points.com, meaning they don’t count as a hotel purchase for the purposes of credit card spending. That means if you pay with an IHG credit card, you wouldn’t earn any bonus rewards, so it’s not treated as if it’s IHG spending.

Therefore I’d recommend using a card on which you’re trying to reach a minimum spending requirement, or otherwise, a credit card that maximizes your return on everyday spending. See this post for more on which credit cards are best for buying points.

IHG One Rewards has dynamic award pricing, which means there’s no minimum or maximum number of points a hotel stay can cost. Rather, the cost of an award stay generally correlates somewhat to the cost of a revenue stay.

However, that doesn’t necessarily mean you’ll get the same value with all hotel stays. There are many situations where you can get outsized value by buying points and then redeeming them. Let me just give a few examples, using stays I pulled up for random dates (again, pricing is dynamic, so this won’t reflect what you see every day).

For example, the Six Senses Kyoto is bookable for 165,000 points per night, and you could purchase those points for $825.

That represents massive savings over the cash cost, which is $1,493.

On the other end of the spectrum, the Holiday Inn Express & Suites Tampa is bookable for 33,000 points per night, and you could purchase those points for $165.

That represents massive savings over the cash cost, which is $230.

However, this won’t always be a good deal. For example, take the Kimpton Tres Rios in Playa del Carmen is bookable for 104,000 points per night, and you could purchase those points for $520.

That’s not a good deal compared to the cash cost, which is $429, so there you’d be better off just paying cash directly.

Another thing to keep in mind is that select IHG co-branded credit cards offer free night awards, and those are worth up to a certain number of points. What’s great is that these free night awards can typically be topped off with points, so there could be merit to buying IHG points so that you have points with which to top off these certificates.

You’ll get the most value from your IHG points if you have The Brand New IHG One Rewards Premier Select Credit Card (learn more), The New IHG One Rewards Premier Credit Card (learn more), and The New IHG One Rewards Business Credit Card (learn more).

That’s because the cards offer a fourth night free benefit, meaning that you can book a four night award stay for the cost of three nights. This is essentially the equivalent of 25% off in increments of four nights, since you can use this benefit an unlimited number of times.

Just to use the Six Senses Kyoto example above, if you earned 495,000 points (worth $2,475 at 0.5 cents per point), that would be enough for four nights with the fourth night free. That represents an absolutely massive discount.

IHG has over 15 hotel brands, so there are lots of options for redeeming your IHG One Rewards points. IHG points can be redeemed at the following properties, among others:

Everyone will value points differently. Based on my latest miles & points valuations, I consider IHG points to be worth 0.5 cents each, and I tend to value points pretty conservatively. So the purchase price is around what I value these points.

For non-elite members, IHG One Rewards points expire after 12 months of inactivity. However, any sort of points earning or redemption activity would reset the expiration of your points. Furthermore, IHG One Rewards points don’t expire for elite members in the program.

Keep in mind that IHG elite status is quite easy to earn. Just for having The Brand New IHG One Rewards Premier Select Credit Card (learn more) or The New IHG One Rewards Business Credit Card (learn more), you receive Platinum status, without any sort of a spending requirement.

IHG One Rewards doesn’t have blackout dates on award nights, but the program does have capacity controls. What this means is that some number of standard rooms will be made available for award redemptions every night, but that doesn’t mean that all standard rooms are available for award redemptions.

IHG One Rewards is offering a sale on purchased points. Through November 15, 2026, IHG One Rewards is offering a promotion, and members seem to be eligible for a 100% bonus, which is an opportunity to buy points for 0.5 cents each.

There are instances where buying points can save you over 50% on the cost of a luxury hotel stay. I also think there’s value in having a “reserve” of IHG points, given the brand’s global footprint. You can get even more value out of buying IHG points in conjunction with a premium IHG credit card, so you can get a fourth night free on award redemptions.

#6130. Bank Of America’s No Annual Fee Card Pays 6% In Year One — Here’s The Best Way To Use It

The Bank of America® Customized Cash Rewards credit card pays 6% back in a category you choose during your first year, with no annual fee. That can include online shopping, phone and internet bills, or home repairs. Bank of America® Customized Cash Rewards‘ initial bonus offer is a $200 online cash rewards bonus after you make at least $1,000 in purchases in the first 90 days of account opening. I like finding worthwhile cards outside the familiar bank discussions. More competition is good, and a card can deserve some of your spending without replacing everything else in your wallet. What The Card Currently Offers The standard consumer card has: No annual fee. A $200 initial bonus after $1,000 in purchases within 90 days of account opening. 6% in your selected category during the first year: the normal 3% plus a temporary extra 3%. 2% at grocery stores and wholesale clubs. 1% on other purchases. The higher rates all share a $2,500 quarterly spending allowance; once you’ve used it, those purchases earn 1% too. Banking relationship bonuses can increase earning. For the choice earning category, you can select among gas and electric vehicle charging; online shopping, including cable, internet, phone plans and streaming; dining; travel; drug stores and pharmacies; or home improvement and furnishings. You can change your category once each calendar month for future purchases. Leave it alone and your selection carries forward. It starts out as gas and charging, so someone getting the card for online shopping needs to change that setting. You don’t have to leave $100,000 sitting in a checking account. #6129. The Don Jr. Wedding May Be the Emblem of a Corrupt Age

‘Hogs get slaughtered,’ as the old saying goes — people will tolerate graft only up to a point.

Donald Trump Jr. and his wife, Bettina Anderson, disembark from Air Force One at Dublin Airport in Dublin, Ireland, September 12, 2026.

On May 31, 1871, William Marcy Tweed threw a spectacularly lavish wedding for his daughter, Mary Amelia, in New York City. “Boss” Tweed was then at the height of his power as the political master of New York City, its ruling Democratic Party, and its Tammany Hall machine. Elected to the U.S. House at 29 in 1852, he sacrificed his career in Washington to vote for the Kansas–Nebraska Act, which was massively unpopular in the North. This was not a stance on principle: The vote was a test of party loyalty, and the Pierce administration paid off Tweed by appointing a friend to a job as postmaster. Returning home to New York, Tweed was running Tammany Hall by 1858.

The corruption he oversaw was immense. It at least doubled the cost of building anything that the city could touch. The Tweed Courthouse cost some $13-14 million to build, twice the cost of the Alaska Purchase during the same period. David McCullough argued in The Great Bridge that the Brooklyn Bridge would never have been completed had the Tweed Ring not fallen early in its construction. Tweed and his cronies were convicted of stealing tens of millions of dollars — some modern estimates place the real amount in the hundreds of millions — which would be worth billions today. Alfred Ely Beach, who published Scientific American, decided to build a pioneering subway line between 1868 and 1870, powered by an immense pneumatic tube, and to avoid paying off Tweed, he built it like a bank heist, removing the dirt at night and not telling the city what he was building until it was ready for passengers.

Dan McLaughlin is a senior writer at National Review Online and a fellow at National Review Institute.

#6128. Who should (and shouldn’t) get the United Quest Card?

The Brand New IHG One Rewards Premier Select Credit Card

Earn up to $4,300 in travel value when you spend $120,000 in your first 4 months as a cardholder

As High As 175,000 points. Find Out Your Offer.

If you fly United Airlines regularly, the (see rates and fees) can be a powerful way to earn more miles and reduce your out-of-pocket travel costs.

As someone who frequently flies United, I've found that the Quest hits a practical middle ground. It offers meaningful airline perks, including a $200 annual United TravelBank credit, two free checked bags and discounts on award flights, without the hefty annual fee of a premium airline card.

But with a $350 annual fee, the Quest isn't necessarily right for everyone.

Here's who I think can get the most value from the card and who might be better off with another option.

Related: I just changed my airline loyalty — here's how the United Quest Card sealed the switch

New United Quest cardholders can currently earn 500 PQP after their first purchase and 80,000 bonus miles after spending $4,000 on purchases in the first three months from account opening. Plus, you can earn another 10,000 bonus miles after adding an authorized user in the first three months from account opening.

Based on TPG's November 2026 valuations, which peg United miles at 1.2 cents apiece, the full 90,000-mile bonus is worth $1,080. That's not including the additional value of the 500 PQP, which can help you get closer to United Premier status.

While not the strongest offer we've seen in the card's history, it's still a great time to apply if you've already been considering the Quest, particularly if you have upcoming United travel planned.

There's a lot to love about the . Here's who will benefit most from having the card.

If you fly United several times per year, you'll want to take a closer look at the Quest.

That’s because many of the card’s most valuable perks are tied directly to flying United. Cardholders receive:

One of the card's strongest perks is its earning structure. The United Quest earns a strong 10 total miles per dollar spent on eligible United flights as a United MileagePlus member — that's a whopping 12% return, according to TPG's valuations (mileage earning may differ for basic economy and base option tickets).

As someone who holds Premier Silver status, I can earn a total of 12 miles per dollar spent on eligible United flights when using my Quest, which is an even better return.

But what I find especially valuable are the discounts United cardholders now receive when booking award flights. Eligible United cardholders without Premier status save at least 10% on qualifying United-operated award flights, while cardholders with Premier status save at least 15%.

I take advantage of these discounts pretty regularly. Recently, I booked two tickets from Washington, D.C.'s Dulles International Airport (IAD) to London's Heathrow Airport (LHR) for a mother-daughter trip to Europe. Thanks to my cardholder discount, each ticket cost just 34,000 miles plus $11.20 in taxes and fees, rather than 45,000 miles plus taxes and fees.

That's a savings of 11,000 miles per ticket, or 22,000 miles total, worth $264 according to TPG's valuations.

The Quest also offers two additional award flight discounts: 10,000 miles beginning with your first card anniversary and another 10,000 miles after spending $20,000 on purchases in a calendar year.

I recently used my 10,000-mile award flight discount toward a transatlantic flight from Amsterdam Airport Schiphol (AMS) to IAD. The flight would have cost 34,000 miles, but the credit brought it down to just 24,000 miles plus $112.83 in taxes and fees.

That's another $120 worth of miles saved, based on TPG's valuations.

Between the cardholder award pricing discounts and the annual award flight credits, the Quest gives me several ways to stretch my United miles further, which is why it's a card I plan to keep in my wallet long-term.

Related: United unveils huge MileagePlus shake-up, rewarding cardholders with higher earn rates

This is one of the most underrated — and potentially most valuable — perks of the United Quest Card.

The card includes two free checked bags for you and a companion on the same reservation. On domestic economy flights, United typically charges $50 ($45 if prepaid) for the first checked bag and $60 ($55 if prepaid) for the second bag.

That means you could pay up to $110 per person each way if you check two bags without a card benefit.

If you and a companion each check two bags round-trip on just one domestic flight, that could cost up to $440 total. That alone covers the Quest Card’s $350 annual fee.

Personally, I frequently fly United and regularly check two bags free thanks to my Quest Card. For travelers who often travel with a companion, don’t pack light, take longer trips or occasionally travel with bulkier items like skis or golf clubs, this benefit alone can justify holding the card year after year.

Related: These 27 credit cards can get you free checked bags on your next flight

Each account anniversary, the Quest Card provides $200 in United TravelBank cash. This credit can be used toward United-operated flights and is automatically deposited into your TravelBank account.

I recently used my $200 TravelBank credit to offset the cost of a round-trip flight from San Francisco International Airport (SFO) to IAD to visit family. The ticket originally cost $560, but my TravelBank credit brought my out-of-pocket cost down to $360.

And the TravelBank credit isn't the only statement credit available with the Quest.

Cardholders can also receive other statement credits, including:

I wouldn't go out of my way to use a credit just to justify the card's annual fee, but if you're already spending money with these merchants, they can provide some additional savings.

For me, the TravelBank credit is the easiest to use. When you subtract its $200 value from the Quest's $350 annual fee, that leaves an effective cost of $150 — assuming you can use the credit in full — before factoring in free checked bags, award flight discounts and other benefits.

If you're working toward United Premier status, the Quest Card can also help you get there.

Cardholders can earn 1 PQP for every $20 spent on purchases with the card, up to 18,000 PQP per calendar year.

Those PQP count toward United Premier status qualification, potentially helping you close the gap to your next status tier.

Plus, beginning in 2027, eligible United cardholders will receive a head start on status qualification. United will deposit PQP equivalent to 5% of the amount required for their current Premier status tier into their accounts at the start of the year. That means Premier Silver members, for example, will receive a 300-PQP boost.

I earned United Premier Silver status for the first time last year, and I've already secured it again for next year, thanks in part to the PQP boost I received at the beginning of the year and the PQP I've earned through flying and spending on my Quest.

I generally don't put much spending on the card outside of United purchases, since I have other cards that earn more flexible rewards on everyday expenses. However, I did intentionally increase my Quest spending over the past few months to earn the additional PQP I needed to secure Silver for another year.

For me, that was worth it because I regularly fly United and appreciate the benefits that come with Premier status.

Of course, I wouldn't recommend putting unnecessary purchases on a card just to earn PQP. But if you're already close to qualifying for status, the Quest can give you another way to get there.

The United Quest Card is a strong step up from the (see rates and fees) — especially for travelers who fly United more than once or twice per year.

The Explorer is a great entry-level option, with a $0 introductory annual fee for the first year (then $150) and useful perks like a free checked bag and two one-time United Club passes each year. For occasional United flyers, that may be all you need.

But if you’re booking multiple United flights annually and check bags or redeem miles, the Quest’s incremental perks can quickly outweigh the difference in annual fees and deliver stronger long-term value.

In short, the Explorer fits the occasional flyer. The Quest is designed for frequent United travelers who can maximize its recurring value.

While the is packed with benefits for United fans and frequent travelers, there are a few reasons why the card might not be the right fit. Let's take a deeper look at who the card isn't the right fit for.

While the United Quest Card has many travel-related benefits, it does not come with any lounge privileges, and you don’t get any guest passes.

If lounge access is a priority, the (see rates and fees) may be a better fit. It includes a United Club membership as part of its annual fee, which grants access for the primary cardholder and eligible guests.

And for those who don't want to pay the United Club's steep $695 annual fee, remember that the offers two guest passes annually for a much more approachable fee ($0 introductory; $150 after the first year).

That said, not everyone needs airline-specific lounge access. For example, I personally get lounge access through the Capital One Venture X Rewards Credit Card, so I don’t need the Quest Card to provide that benefit.

While the number of Capital One lounges is limited, the Venture X also includes a Priority Pass lounge membership (at participating lounges), so I rarely feel short on options.

If you also already have lounge access through another premium travel card, the lack of United Club access here may not matter.

Related: Is the United Club Card annual fee worth it?

The United Quest Card is subject to Chase’s 5/24 rule. If you’ve opened five or more personal credit cards across all issuers in the past 24 months, you’re unlikely to be approved.

If you’re currently over 5/24, you may need to wait — or consider a card from another issuer.

Related: Chase's 5/24 rule: Everything you need to know

The United Quest Card earns United MileagePlus miles. If you don’t regularly fly United — or you prefer more flexibility in how you redeem your rewards — a transferable points or miles card could be a better option.

Flexible points and miles can typically be transferred to multiple airline and hotel partners or redeemed in other ways, giving you more options.

Two strong alternatives with significantly lower annual fees include:

If you value flexibility over airline-specific perks, one of those cards may be a better long-term fit.

If you fly United multiple times per year, check bags regularly and can easily use the $200 annual TravelBank credit, the United Quest Card’s ongoing perks can quickly offset much of its $350 annual fee.

However, if you prioritize lounge access, prefer flexible points or miles over airline-specific miles or only fly United occasionally, another card — either within United’s lineup or outside of it — may be a better fit.

Ultimately, the Quest Card shines for travelers who are loyal enough to United to benefit from its airline perks but don’t need the full premium treatment of a club membership.

#6126. Etihad Slashes Flights, Pulls Airbus A380 Off Two Routes (Including Toronto)

Etihad Airways has just filed a major schedule update for early 2027, impacting a couple of dozen routes. In isolation, you might not think much of this, as the first several weeks of the year have weaker demand in many markets. However, in light of what’s going on in Etihad’s commercial division, I can’t help but be curious if there’s a bit more to this, and wonder how things will evolve.

AeroRoutes reports on how Abu Dhabi-based Etihad has filed a schedule change for the first quarter of 2027, with most of the changes taking place for flights as of January 11, 2027. For the most part, the reductions are for around a couple of months, through March 2027. There are two ways to look at this:

The frequency reductions we’re seeing are pretty significant. Just to look at service to North America:

Specific to the A380, it seems that Etihad is taking the jet off the Toronto and Singapore (SIN) routes over that period, and it doesn’t seem like the super jumbo will be flying any other routes in place of that, at least based on current schedule filings. During that period, Etihad will only be flying the A380 to four destinations — Bangkok (BKK), London (LHR), Paris (CDG), and Tokyo Narita (NRT).

It’s a fascinating time for Etihad. Obviously Gulf carriers are having a rather difficult time with everything going on in the region at the moment, and it comes at a unique time for Etihad, as the carrier has been going through a massive expansion.

Now, I’ve been a bit skeptical about the claimed economics of this expansion, but Etihad management has insisted everything couldn’t be better… until Etihad Chief Commercial Officer Arik De recently “departed” the airline.

The can of worms that this departure opened is truly unlike anything I’ve seen at any airline before… and I’ve been following this industry for a long time. Seriously, check out the 520+ comments on my post about his departure, because employees have a lot to say. It’s so salacious that it has gotten OMAAT blocked in the UAE.

The point is, if even a quarter of the things are to be believed — and I’ve had some very interesting conversations with some formerly very high up people at the airline — then the carrier’s entire commercial strategy has been a bit questionable, to put it politely, and more about serving a certain someone’s LinkedIn profile ego, rather than actually developing a commercial strategy.

So with him no longer there, I’m curious to see how this all evolves. Let me emphasize that this is of course in no way a knock on all the hardworking employees at Etihad who have had to endure this “leadership” for too long. It seems like they now have quite the web to untangle, especially given the toxic people who are reportedly still there.

Etihad Airways has just filed a pretty big schedule change for early 2027, whereby a couple of dozen routes are seeing significant capacity reductions. Most notably, the Airbus A380 is being taken off of both the Toronto and Singapore routes.

In isolation, you might not think much of this, as demand is often a little lighter earlier in the year. But what I find interesting is that this follows a period of very rapid expansion, along with the carrier’s head of commercial strategy getting the boot.

Based on what I’ve heard from a countless number of current and former Etihad management employees, the strategy of the past couple of years hasn’t been as sound as a certain someone has tried to make it appear. We’ll see how this all unravels.

What do you make of this Etihad schedule change, and how do you see things playing out?

#6125. United Airlines CEO Scott Kirby Bans AI Agents From Booking Tickets, Doesn’t Want “Another Middleman”

“To be honest, I don’t want to create another middleman.”

I get that they want to negotiate the terms before a new company gets between United and its customers. But United can’t just decide that customers will have to do the work themselves and expect that all customers will go ahead and do the work to buy tickets from United when it becomes easier just to buy from someone else. And writing a ban into a contract doesn’t mean United can actually identify an AI booking that comes through Expedia.

United’s November 11 contract of carriage revision adds AI agents to its prohibited ticketing practices. Rule 6.J.6 bans: The use of AI Agents to make, modify or service a Ticket, and/or to purchase any service or product. The definition includes assistants accessing United through a travel agency or another intermediary. Human supervision or approval doesn’t circumvent that. And its Rule 5.H gives United the right to cancel reservations made, modified or serviced by these agents. The Wall Street Journal says agents can still present United flights and prices. AI research, followed by the customer making a purchase on their own, doesn’t run afoul of United’s rules. United Wouldn’t Know If An AI Agent Bought Through Expedia? Expedia already has a ChatGPT integration. It returns flight and hotel options with prices and availability. Expedia’s current instructions then send the customer to Expedia to complete the purchase. It’s not an autonomous purchase inside ChatGPT, but if an agent completes the purchase on Expedia United just sees an Expedia booking not how the booking was made. United says its systems can identify booking sources. Sure, but that is a non-sequitur. A contractual ban isn’t a technical one. United may push intermediaries to enforce the restriction, but there are lots of intermediaries out there. But we’ve seen airlines go to war with online travel agencies before, cutting off their own sales. The Strongest Case For United Is About Bargaining Power United may want to limit access to its sysems: The next middleman could become expensive. An assistant that decides which flights customers see can eventually demand referral fees, sell placement or favor suppliers that agree to its terms. Sam Altman says that if an AI does this, no one will trust it, and the stakes are too high to compromise trust for a travel commission. Someone has to own the mistakes. An agent can buy the wrong dates, misunderstand a fare restriction or cancel a ticket the customer wanted to keep. Agencies have commercial arrangements for ticketing and servicing. An AI assistant operating a browser may not bring the same accountability. And the law is evolving here. I’ve covered Delta’s own AI canceling a return flight it said it would preserve. Delta acknowledged a bug and restored the itinerary. Shopping consumes resources even when nobody buys. An agent can compare far more combinations than a human. The International Air Transport Association has examined the cost of growing search volumes. But United isn’t banning search, just completing the transaction. United can do this now, but it won’t last. The airline says agent bookings are still rare. That makes this a relatively inexpensive time to withhold permission. Every customer who gets used to buying another airline through an assistant becomes harder to win back. And the same customers most likely to use an AI assistant are the ones most likely to come over to United for Starlink. United has a hub in San Francisco. It’s ultimately not going to work for Scott Kirby to stand athwart history yelling “stop!” Customers Have A Reason To Hire The Bot United’s safety argument is weak. The federal hazardous-materials rule requires passenger notices, including at ticket purchase where practical and at check-in, and passenger acknowledgment in self-service transactions. It doesn’t require the customer to manually complete every other step of a booking. An assistant can stop and ask the passenger to review a disclosure or give a required confirmation. United’s definition still covers an agent whose actions the customer supervises and approves. Nor does accepting an agent have to mean giving unfamiliar software unrestricted use of a MileagePlus password. Visa is developing ways for merchants to recognize approved agents and connect their actions with customer and payment information. The customer’s time is part of the cost of buying a flight. If I can tell an assistant my dates, preferred airports, seat requirements and budget, there’s value in having it compare the choices and handle the purchase. Sometimes United’s schedule will be good enough that consumers will do the extra work. Sometimes another airline will offer a comparable trip and let an assistant finish it. We’ve already seen an airline overestimate its ability to make customers use its preferred distribution channels. American backed away from its plan to deny mileage earning on certain travel agency bookings. Customers didn’t all abandon the agencies and processes they preferred just because American wanted them to. There’s also an obvious reason airlines might dislike an assistant that works well for the passenger. It can compare the total price, recognize benefits the customer already gets from status or a credit card, and decline add-ons that aren’t worth buying. United has the worst value prop of any U.S. airline for basic economy! I’ve made the same argument about rewards credit cards: companies are excited about using AI to sell more, but customers get better tools too. #6123. Cathay Pacific Orders 41 Airbus A330-900neos, As New Regional Workhorse

In August 2024, Cathay Pacific placed an order for 30 Airbus A330neos. There’s now an update, as the airline has just bumped this order by 11 more planes, meaning that there are now a total of 41 of these aircraft on order. Let’s take a look at all the details, and discuss what this means for fleet modernization at the Hong Kong based oneworld carrier.

Cathay Pacific now has a firm order for 41 Airbus A330-900neo aircraft, which are expected to be delivered between 2028 and 2035.

This follows an evaluation of the carrier’s mid-size wide body fleet renewal program, and it will enable Cathay Pacific to modernize its earlier generation A330-300 fleet, and expand its operations on high capacity regional routes. However, the airline is leaving plans for this plane open, and also emphasizes how the jet offers the flexibility to serve longer range destinations.

For those not familiar, the A330neo is the updated version of the A330, featuring improved range and fuel efficiency. The A330-900neo is the larger of the two new variants (with the other being the A330-800neo). The plane has a range of 7,200 nautical miles, plus a capacity for 287 passengers in a standard three cabin configuration.

I think it’s safe to assume that at least most of these A330neos will be equipped with the new Aria Studio business class product, which is expected to be retrofitted on select existing A330s in the coming months. This will finally see the carrier introduce a dedicated regional product with flat beds, which is exciting, though it’s not quite to the level of the long haul Aria Suite business class.

Here’s how Cathay Pacific CEO Ronald Lam described how the A330neo fits into the carrier’s fleet, back when the first 30 frames were ordered:

“The A330 is an aircraft type that has been serving Cathay Pacific well for nearly 30 years. These new aircraft will principally serve our regional destinations in Asia, while also providing the flexibility to serve longer-haul destinations as required. The improved fuel efficiency of these A330neos, together with their high standards of comfort, will enable us to further elevate the experience we provide for our customers while also contributing towards our goal of net-zero carbon emissions by 2050.”

Cathay Pacific refreshing its short and medium haul fleet with the Airbus A330-900neo makes perfect sense, and is just about the safest, most expected aircraft order that Cathay Pacific could place. For context on Cathay Pacific’s fleet, the airline has:

Now Cathay Pacific’s fleet renewal plans are becoming a bit clearer, as the airline has:

So a decade down the road, you can expect that Cathay Pacific will primarily be flying A321neos, A330-900neos, A350s (-900s and -1000s), and 777-9s. That seems like a pretty logical fleet development plan to me.

Cathay Pacific now has an order for 41 Airbus A330-900neos, which the airline will primarily use to modernize and grow its regional fleet. The carrier already flies A330-300s, some of which are nearly 25 years old, so it’s logical that the airline would slowly be looking to replace these jets.

Cathay Pacific now has a pretty impressive (but not overly ambitious) order book, with A321neos, A330-900neos, and 777-9s, used for fleet renewal.

What do you make of Cathay Pacific’s Airbus A330-900neo order?
