#6121. ICE Checked 7 White Men’s IDs At The Airport—Then Arrested A State Trooper

Two ICE agents spent nearly an hour at the Madison, Wisconsin airport looking for a state trooper. Before finding him, they approached at least seven other white men and checked their IDs. Then they handcuffed the 21-year old officer, who had federal permission to work through 2030 and was flying to visit his parents. Newly released surveillance footage shows how the November 5 arrest unfolded. Carel Aaron Van Der Merwe was released the following evening after a Republican congressman contacted the Homeland Security secretary. He still faces immigration proceedings. They Went Looking For White People! In Wisconson! The two immigration agents wore baseball caps and hoodies, with no obvious identification on their clothing. They carried manila folders and consulted papers while looking for someone matching Van Der Merwe’s description. The agents approached seven white men visible in the recording, plus another person outside the camera’s view. The men generally looked young, wore everything from sweatpants to business casual, and mostly carried backpacks. They produced ID and were allowed to continue. Two uniformed deputies waited with the agents. Once their target arrived, he handed over identification, spoke with the agents and walked with them to the airport’s entrance doors. An agent handcuffed him there. Van Der Merwe explained that he had a work permit and a pending asylum application, and the agents said they “did not care.” The Government Had Authorized Him To Work Van Der Merwe’s parents brought him from South Africa in March 2019, when he was 14. His original admission permitted a six month stay. His attorney says the family applied for asylum and has spent seven years waiting for an interview. He’s included in his father’s application and holds federal employment authorization through 2030. According to his attorney, he wanted to join the military but couldn’t because of his immigration status. He earned a criminal justice degree at New Mexico Military Institute and went into law enforcement instead. He’s been with the Wisconsin State Patrol since July 13, 2025 He was work-authorized by the federal government but that’s also consistent with a visa overstay, as I explained when ICE arrested Southwest Airlines flight attendant Lorenzo Thompson at Nashville airport. A person can have an unresolved asylum claim, hold a valid employment authorization document, and still face removal proceedings. That’s a pretty upside down world, since the government said he could work here and should allow him to stay pending resolution of asylum – which he’s been waiting for the government to address for years. Homeland Security says Van Der Merwe overstayed his original admission. His lawyer says he’s followed the legal process and has been waiting for the government to decide his case. Federal law allows detention while a removal case is pending. Prior to the Trump administration, a work-authorized individual with a pending asylum claim was essentially considered to be in valid status, and ICE hasn’t alleged any separate crime. The government knows where he lives and works, in a role promoting public safety, so it’s not clear what benefit there is to taking him off a family trip and putting him in jail while his asylum claim remains unresolved. The President now says his approach to immigration has been too harsh. Q: You think your deportation policy went too far? Trump: I think it might be too tough. https://t.co/NKhFjZKxnd — Clash Report (@clashreport) November 8, 2026 Airports Make People Easy To Find TSA likely alerted ICE when he bought his ticket. A May 2025 agreement obtained by American Oversight formalized information sharing between TSA and ICE, including storage of information by ICE. As I wrote in July, passenger information collected for aviation security is being used to locate immigration targets. Homeland Security says it considers people unlawfully present “can no longer fly unless it is out of our country to self-deport.” An airline reservation tells the government where someone plans to be and when. That makes an airport a convenient place to arrest them. But using TSA this way becomes a distraction from its security focus. We’ve already seen a U.S. citizen handcuffed while boarding Delta after being mistaken for a British man, and plainclothes agents abandon an attempted arrest at Las Vegas airport, leaving a traveler with a handcuff attached. Van Der Merwe went to jail and was released November 6 without posting bond after Representative Derrick Van Orden contacted Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin. Homeland Security says it considers people unlawfully present “can no longer fly unless it is out of our country to self-deport.” An airline reservation tells the government where someone plans to be and when. That makes an airport a convenient place to arrest them. But using TSA this way becomes a distraction from its security focus.

Translation: I got my arse handed to me on Tuesday so we will take revenge but if caught: “the agents are at fault”.

And this is a surprise? Make a quota, get to stay a masked armed agent who can drag people off the street. And of course they didn’t care! “The New Yorker” just had an article about border agents who couldn’t take it anymore. Those who stayed just shut down and did what they were told. Maybe most governments run like that, but they do better having systems with some kind of sense and humanity.

There is no place for a secret police force in a so-called free country. Conservatives and libertarians once believed in limited government and personal freedom. That seems to be all forgotten in the race to see who can hate immigrants more.

The whole administration approach with quotas is just wrong.

Every administration has kicked the immigration law revisions can down the road.

The US is long overdue for a comprehensive and integrated immigration policy review and update.

Just another episode in the idiotic, nonsensical world of Trump. How about deporting Elon instead? He’s a far greater threat to this country than a state trooper risking his life to keep citizens safe.

@drrichard — “But, but… the leopards won’t eat MY face…” — That state trooper, probably.

Our immigration enforcement is out of control. Masked storm troopers roaming the streets and airports demanding “show me your papers” because they think you look like someone? It’s like out of some Cold War spy movie, except those goons aren’t masked.

And don’t claim that you have a big concern about “following the rules” especially if you think a man who sexually assaulted a woman in a department store dressing room and has 34 felony convictions should be President of the United States. Or if you hire gardeners, maids and other domestic workers without verifying their immigration status.

The money and effort expended in this indiscriminate, xenophobic hysteria makes no sense. Reform immigration and immigration enforcement.

And this is why I left some blood in Vietnam? “WHAT A COUNTRY”.

It's a question we've been diving deep into at The Points Guy this month (and something we've been debating for years now). Not only has it been harder to get upgrades and more expensive to earn status, but redemptions have gotten more expensive and watered-down benefits have made pursuing status less appealing for many of us at The Points Guy.

But not me. Despite my complaints, I'm still a fan of top-tier status and can't quit the hamster wheel, though I'm not trying for quite so many these days.

I've already requalified for World of Hyatt Globalist status this year, and I'll be able to requalify for top-tier American Airlines AAdvantage status. But I will also hold lower-tier status with United MileagePlus, Alaska Airlines' Atmos Rewards program and Delta SkyMiles.

In 2027, I'll continue to hold Platinum Elite status in IHG One Rewards and Marriott Bonvoy, as well as Hilton Honors Diamond status and Air Canada Aeroplan 25K status, just for carrying credit cards.

I even have top-tier status with Starbucks Rewards.

Here's the full breakdown of my elite-status plans for 2027, the credit cards I use to fast-track them, plus some tips to help you achieve your own status goals before the end of the year.

I've held top-tier American Airlines AAdvantage Executive Platinum status on and off for years now. I'm already getting closer to requalifying for 2027, and since the qualification year runs through Feb. 28, I have a few more months to work toward my goal.

So far, I've earned 148,538 Loyalty Points — the metric that AAdvantage members must accrue to earn elite status — toward the 200,000 Loyalty Points required to qualify for the Executive Platinum tier. Once I hit that threshold, I'll requalify for perks like a 120% mileage bonus, Group 1 boarding, complimentary food and drinks when traveling in the main cabin and more.

Related: 5 ways to earn more American Airlines Loyalty Points before February ends

Thanks to the airline's Loyalty Point Rewards milestones, I can also hit a few more reward tiers along the way to Executive Platinum status. For example, once I hit 175,000 Loyalty Points, I can choose from a menu of valuable benefits, including two systemwide upgrade certificates.

I'm likely to choose systemwide upgrades again, but the 25,000 bonus miles and the trip credits are probably the best alternate options.

I've already used two systemwide upgrades from coach to business class on AA's transcontinental flight from San Francisco to New York and back. I also just confirmed two more upgrades for upcoming international trips, including a flight to Paris from New York and another from London back to New York.

Holding the (see rates and fees) makes it easier to rack up Loyalty Points. This card helps me reach my status goal by netting me up to 40,000 additional Loyalty Points per elite status qualification year (10,000 bonus Loyalty Points after reaching 50,000, 90,000, 165,000 and 240,000 Loyalty Points).

Related: How I booked Japan Airlines first class for just 80K American Airlines AAdvantage miles

Alaska Airlines Atmos Rewards is now the only major U.S. airline loyalty program that lets you earn elite status from actual flight miles. That means you don't have to spend an outrageous amount of money to earn top-tier status (though you can choose to earn status via spending). Alaska Atmos Rewards members can now also earn points on award redemptions, which has driven my status earnings this year.

I've spent my Atmos Rewards points on award tickets flying Cathay Pacific within Asia and a flight from Seattle to Hong Kong in business class, a Hawaiian Airlines first-class flight from Honolulu to New York and an American Airlines flight from New York to Prague.

So far, I've earned the 40,000 status points required for Gold status this year through a combination of reward flights and spending on my . In addition to earning 1 status point for every $2 spent, with no spending cap, I also earn 10,000 status points each year on my account anniversary and 3 points per $1 on all foreign transactions with this card. This makes it worth the $395 annual fee, to me.

(Cardholders with the $95 annual fee earn 1 status point per $3 spent, also with no spending cap.)

While Alaska's partnership with American Airlines means I can fly Alaska flights with my top-tier American Airlines AAdvantage status, I'm considering pursuing an even higher Alaska status in 2027. One of the main reasons is that Alaska upgrades its top-tier Titanium members (and a companion) to business class on international flights on the day of departure. Those with status are also now eligible for complimentary upgrades on Hawaiian Airlines flights. I've gotten upgraded on Hawaiian a few times with my status.

I'm also putting a ton of spending on my Summit card now, since Atmos Rewards has a partnership with Bilt that gets you 3 Atmos Rewards points for every dollar of rent you put on the card.

All that spending could help get me a good chunk of the way toward top-tier Titanium status, which requires 135,000 status points. I need to make a decision soon about my 2027 focus, but I haven't been able to cut the cord with American Airlines and fully commit to Alaska... at least not yet.

Related: Last-minute strategies for earning Alaska Atmos Rewards elite status

Over the past few years, my status with Delta has been on a steep decline. I enjoyed several years as a Delta Diamond, but it's just become too expensive (28,000 Medallion Qualification Dollars, to be exact) to earn top-tier status.

I only qualified for entry-level Silver last year, which requires 5,000 MQDs. A friend threw me a bone and gifted me second-tier Gold status, which typically requires 10,000 MQDs, but I'm not on track to re-earn it for 2027.

So far, my total spending this year is just 7,338 MQDs. This includes 5,000 MQDs just for holding the and the .

The $650 annual fee (see rates and fees) for the Delta Reserve is steep, but it's often worth it for those chasing status. It's just not enough of a boost to get me even to Gold status.

The Reserve card does give 1 MQD for every $10 you spend on the card. Technically, you could spend your way to status, but there's no way I can put that much spending on my Delta SkyMiles Reserve American Express Card. While I still like the card for all its perks, I'm no longer putting much spending on it.

While I am likely to drop down to Silver for 2027, I'll still fly Delta occasionally.

I've made great use of SkyMiles over the years. Last year, I lucked out with an award from Mexico City International Airport (MEX) to Los Angeles International Airport (LAX) and then to Brisbane Airport (BNE) in Delta One. There was a brief moment when the flight was available for just 73,000 SkyMiles one-way. I jumped at the opportunity to fly in Delta One on the more-than-14-hour flight to Australia.

Despite being what I'd consider the least valuable airline currency, SkyMiles remain appealing, and I'll keep my Reserve and Platinum cards for the long term. I've gotten a lot of use out of the statement credits that come with holding the cards.

Related: Last-minute strategies for earning Delta Medallion elite status

I added another airline elite status to my collection in 2026: Air Canada Aeroplan 25K status, which I received simply for signing up for the (see rates and fees) and carrying the card. This would typically require earning 25,000 Status Qualifying Credits through the airline.

Unfortunately, I haven't had many opportunities to actually fly with Air Canada, and I've even let some of my valuable eUpgrade credits expire unused.

Still, I've become increasingly interested in the Air Canada Aeroplan program, especially because of its extensive network of airline partners and the ability to book some excellent business-class award flights through them.

One of my favorite redemptions using my welcome bonus on that card was booking a business-class flight on Emirates from Rio de Janeiro to Buenos Aires for just 56,000 Aeroplan points. It's a fascinating fifth-freedom route, and I was especially excited about the opportunity to finally experience Emirates.

I was also able to book Swiss Airlines business class from Cairo to Zurich and then on to New York for just 85,000 Aeroplan points.

Looking ahead, I'm particularly intrigued by Aeroplan's generous stopover rules. The program allows travelers to add a stopover of more than 24 hours on eligible international one-way award itineraries for just 5,000 additional points. That's an incredible opportunity to visit two destinations on a single award ticket.

Even though I haven't gotten much use out of my Air Canada elite status, Aeroplan remains one of the most interesting airline loyalty programs in my points-and-miles arsenal. I'm hoping to put more of those points — and perhaps some of those elite benefits — to work in the year ahead.

Related: How to redeem Aeroplan points for maximum value

Another new status for me is United Airlines MileagePlus Premier Silver. I actually did a status challenge with United late last year, and enjoyed a few months of top-tier United Premier 1K status, but I wasn't able to complete the challenge to unlock it for a full year.

Still, I've really enjoyed flying United more. It's easier to get to their hub at Newark Liberty International Airport (EWR) from my New York City apartment, and I ended up flying and earning enough this year to earn the entry-level United Silver status, which requires at least 6,000 Premier qualifying points or 15 Premier Qualifying Flights and 5,000 PQPs. (In 2027, United is ditching PQFs, making status eligible only through PQPs.)

Silver status allows me to get priority boarding, extra-legroom seats at check-in 24 hours before flying and standby for earlier flights.

During the brief window I had 1K status, I really enjoyed boarding ahead of Group 1.

Related: 5 last-minute ways to earn United elite status this year

More importantly, during my challenge I signed up for the (see rates and fees), which got me a good stash of United miles that I've used effectively.

I was able to spend just 85,000 United miles for a one-way business-class flight from Tokyo to Chicago and then on to Newark this year, and I've just booked another business-class flight from Sydney, Australia, back to New York for 85,000 United miles.

I've earned a total of 8,640 PQPs toward status this year, but I'm unlikely to earn the more than 3,000 more I'd need for Premier Gold before the end of the year. I think Silver status is just fine for me for now.

I've loved having top-tier World of Hyatt Globalist status again this year. I've been able to use suite upgrades at several stand-out properties this year, including the Grand Hyatt Kauai Resort & Spa in Hawaii, the Grand Hyatt Rio de Janeiro in Brazil and the Hyatt Regency Cairo West in Egypt.

Globalist benefits include guaranteed 4 p.m. late checkout, free breakfast and better upgrade odds.

This year, I've earned top-tier status organically with stays all over the world. I especially loved finally getting to check out the newly renovated Park Hyatt Tokyo and to stay at the Park Hyatts in Shanghai and Beijing.

While earning Globalist status requires 60 nights at Hyatt hotels per year, I've already stayed 79 nights this year. I may try to hit 90 nights in 2026, so I can earn another Milestone Rewards choice.

I also plan on keeping both my (see rates and fees) and my (see rates and fees) to help me get more elite nights toward status each year.

Related: Which credit card should you use for Hyatt stays?

I've also been putting Hyatt stays on my World of Hyatt Credit Card to earn 4 points per dollar spent at Hyatt hotels and resorts. You also earn two elite nights for every $5,000 you put on the personal card.

To me, World of Hyatt is the most valuable hotel loyalty program because I often get upgraded and never have to fight for late checkout. Hyatt points also stretch very far, especially compared with Hilton and Marriott. I already have trips on the books next year for Alila Villas Uluwatu in Indonesia, Park Hyatt Milan and Hyatt Paris Madeleine.

Related: How to redeem Hyatt points for free nights and more

Hilton Honors elite status is one of the easiest achievements to reach. Although I stayed at a Hilton hotel only a few times this year, I maintained Diamond status. How did I manage that? It's a perk of holding .

Related: Last-minute strategies for earning Hilton Honors elite status

The card comes with Hilton Diamond status for as long as you hold it. Despite a $550 annual card fee (see rates and fees), the card is still worth keeping.

There are other valuable inclusions, such as up to $400 to spend at Hilton resorts every year (up to $200 in statement credits from January to June and another up to $200 in statement credits from July to December), up to $200 in statement credits for eligible flight purchases (up to $50 per quarter) and a free night when you open the account and reach your annual card anniversary.

Last year, I used my free night at the chic Conrad Tokyo on a room that would have been more than $1,100. This year, I used it at the Hilton Tokyo in a room that went for more than $650 a night.

I used one of my $200 stay statement credits last year at the Hilton Tangier Al Houara Resort & Spa in Morocco, and the other at Resorts World Las Vegas. In past years, I've also used it at Hilton Cancun Mar Caribe All-Inclusive Resort and Hilton Hawaiian Village Waikiki Beach Resort in Hawaii.

I also use the airline fee credits regularly. When using the Aspire card to pay, you get up to $50 in statement credits for eligible airline purchases each quarter.

Thanks to this card, I've had Hilton Diamond status since 2020.

Related: No suite upgrade but charm aplenty: What it's like staying at one of Hilton's SLH properties as a top-tier elite

While I have had some nice stays at Hilton properties — including the stunning Conrad Bora Bora Nui — over the years, I've rarely been upgraded despite my Diamond status. Still, the statement credits alone justify keeping the Aspire card and my Diamond status for 2027, even if I don't have as much luck getting upgrades with Hilton as I do with Hyatt.

I will earn Platinum Elite status with Marriott again this year just for holding a credit card.

In the past, I've been content with the Marriott Bonvoy Gold Elite status I receive courtesy of the ; it gives status in several hotel programs, including Marriott Bonvoy (enrollment required).

Related: Guide to Marriott and Hilton elite status with the Amex Platinum and Business Platinum

Then in 2022, American Express surprised everyone by announcing that holders of the would get Platinum Elite status for as long as they hold the card. I jumped at the chance to apply for it. As a result, I've held Platinum Elite status since then.

I've spent more than two dozen nights at Marriott properties this year and having Platinum Elite status certainly enhanced my trips with benefits like guaranteed late checkout, lounge access and complimentary breakfast. I even got an upgrade at the Ritz-Carlton in Hong Kong.

I used the annual free night that comes with the Brilliant card two years in a row at the lakefront Hotel President Wilson in Geneva, Switzerland. Last year, I used it for London's Bankside Hotel.

Related: 30 best Marriott hotels in the world that you can book with points

So far, I've booked 46 Marriott nights this year. I won't try to get the higher Titanium status — which requires 75 nights — though the idea of opening the is intriguing. Each year you hold the card, you receive 15 elite night credits toward the next level of Marriott Bonvoy elite status.

At least for now, though, I'll keep the personal Brilliant card open and enjoy Platinum Elite status without worrying about how many nights I need to stay.

Related: Last-minute strategies to earn Marriott Bonvoy elite status

Like my other hotel statuses, I have Platinum Elite status with IHG One Rewards by virtue of holding its hotel-branded card.

Last year, I stayed at several memorable IHG properties, including the Kimpton Fitzroy in London, the InterContinental Porto in Portugal, the Kimpton Overland Hotel in Atlanta and the InterContinental Ljubljana in Slovenia. This year, I've checked into the Hotel InterContinental Bordeaux Le Grand and WM Hotel in Sai Kung (a Vignette property) near Hong Kong.

Despite staying only seven nights at IHG hotels in 2026, I will maintain IHG Platinum Elite status simply by holding the IHG One Rewards Select Credit Card (no longer open to new applicants). In addition to elite status, my favorite perk of this card is its free night award worth up to 40,000 points, which I've used at the Kimpton Armory Hotel in Bozeman, Montana, and the aforementioned InterContinental in Portugal.

The information for the IHG One Rewards Select card has been collected independently by The Points Guy. The card details on this page have not been reviewed or provided by the card issuer.

The new version of the card is the (see rates and fees), which also provides Platinum Elite status. It also comes with a fourth night free on award stays and the ability to add points to your 60,000-point anniversary free night certificate (these perks aren't available on the Select card). The annual fee is $350.

I'll keep my IHG card for status (and a free night) again next year. I'm also sitting on a nice stash of points, so odds are I'll enjoy some great redemptions in the not-too-distant future — though I don't have any IHG stays planned so far in 2027.

Related: Last-minute strategies for earning IHG One Rewards elite status

The last status I'll mention is with Starbucks, since I'm a regular at the cafe near my apartment.

That regularity earned me top-tier Reserve status in the Starbucks Rewards program, which was overhauled earlier this year.

Reserve status earns 0.7 Stars more per dollar spent than entry-level Green status (for a total of 1.7 Stars per dollar) and requires earning an eye-watering 2,500 Stars over a rolling 12-month period to reach. That's 2,000 more Stars than necessary for the next-lowest tier, Gold.

It may not be the most rewarding program in the world — especially if you have a lower status tier — but the savings I get through the program add up and have me just as hooked on it as I am on my preferred hotel and airline programs.

Related: Why I got top-tier status with Starbucks and enjoy it — despite the reduced earnings for some

I've thought about going fully free agent and stopping my pursuit of status. But the truth is, I have fun on the hamster wheel, and the perks really make the game worth playing.

I'll have top-tier status with American, Hyatt and Hilton again next year. I'm excited to use more of my perks in 2027, and I will report back on my 2028 plans next year.

If you're considering going for status, you should really do the math to see if the extra costs are worth the benefits you get. It's harder to earn status these days, and the benefits keep getting whittled down. Don't do it unless you know you will use the perks and that you can do it without spending a small fortune.

It can be more cost-effective to get a credit card that automatically gives you some status perks, like free checked bags and priority boarding.

At least think about it. I'm not sure I'm the best at following my own advice.

#6118. Delta Platinum Amex Card Review: Big Benefits & Strong Welcome Offer

The Delta SkyMiles® Platinum American Express Card is the second most premium personal credit card in the Delta SkyMiles and Amex co-brand card portfolio.

If you fly Delta several times a year and want perks like a companion certificate and the ability to spend toward elite status qualification, the Delta Platinum Amex is worth a look, and can easily be worth more than the fee. This post is my in-depth Delta Platinum Card review, so let’s get into all the details.

Link: Learn more about the Delta SkyMiles® Platinum American Express Card

Before we get too deep into my Delta Platinum Amex review, let me give a quick overview of the card’s main features and fees:

I also put together my top pros and cons for the Delta Platinum SkyMiles Card:

Let’s cover the welcome bonus, eligibility details, and fees, of the Delta Platinum Card. After all, these are major factors that people consider when applying for cards.

The Delta Platinum Card currently has the following welcome offer: You may be eligible for as high as 90,000 Bonus Miles after you spend $3,000 in eligible purchases on your new Card in your first 6 months of Card Membership. Welcome offers vary and you may not be eligible for an offer.

Based on my latest miles & points valuations, SkyMiles are worth 1.1 cents each. That means to me, the welcome bonus is worth up to $990. While Delta SkyMiles is far from my favorite mileage currency, it does have quite a high floor value, so there are good ways to redeem Delta SkyMiles.

The welcome offer on the Delta Platinum Card is “once in a lifetime,” so it’s not available if you currently have the card, or if you’ve had the card in the past. You’re also not eligible for the welcome offer on this card if you have or have had the personal version of the Delta SkyMiles® Reserve American Express Card (learn more). However, you are eligible for this card if you’ve had any version of the business Delta Amex cards before.

One thing worth emphasizing is that if you’re going to apply for multiple personal Delta Amex cards, you’ll want to pick up the less premium cards first, and then work your way up. That way you’re potentially eligible for the welcome offers on each of the cards. Meanwhile if you start with the most premium card, you wouldn’t be eligible for the offers on the less premium cards.

You can read more about Amex’s general application restrictions here.

The Platinum Delta Amex has a $350 annual fee (Rates & Fees). You can add additional users to the card at no extra cost (Rates & Fees). As mentioned above, this is the second highest annual fee personal card in the Delta and Amex portfolio.

If you are going to put spending on the Delta Platinum Amex, the good news is that there are no foreign transaction fees (Rates & Fees), so you can use the card abroad without paying high fees.

When applying for a credit card, the rewards structure is obviously a major consideration for people. With airline credit cards, the question typically comes down to both the miles offered on spending, as well as the ability to qualify for elite status with spending. How does the Delta Platinum Card do on that front? Well, among airline cards, I’d say it’s pretty competitive, so let’s cover those details.

The Delta Platinum Amex offers the following miles earning opportunities for spending:

Since I value Delta miles at 1.1 cents, I think this card offers a 3.3% return on its 3x miles categories (purchases made directly with Delta and directly with hotels), a 2.2% return on its 2x miles categories (restaurants worldwide and U.S. supermarkets), and a 1.1% return on non-bonus spending.

The card has solid bonus categories for a co-branded airline card, but purely in terms of rewards for spending, I think there are still better cards out there for airfare purchases, hotel purchases, restaurant purchases, and grocery store purchases.

Nowadays, Delta SkyMiles Medallion elite status is earned exclusively based on how many Medallion Qualification Dollars (MQDs) you rack up. When it comes to earning MQDs through credit card spending, the Delta Platinum Amex can help you earn status:

For context, Delta SkyMiles Medallion elite status has the following annual MQD requirements:

If you’re serious about earning elite status with credit card spending, you’ll want to consider the more premium Delta SkyMiles® Reserve American Express Card (learn more) instead, since it earns MQDs twice as fast — you earn $1 MQD per $10 of eligible purchases, rather than $1 MQD per $20 of eligible purchases.

While Delta SkyMiles is far from my favorite mileage currency, it does have a high floor value, so there are good ways to redeem Delta SkyMiles. You can redeem SkyMiles for flights on Delta or SkyTeam partners, like Air France, China Airlines, and Korean Air. You can also redeem SkyMiles on airlines like LATAM and WestJet, which aren’t part of SkyTeam.

Partner award flights can be an especially good option if you focus on flights that don’t touch the United States, since flights that do are more expensive and get you less value for your miles. I’ve also seen some good award prices for Delta One (business class) awards, specifically for booking roundtrip rather than one way.

The Platinum Delta Credit Card has a nice welcome offer. In general, I’d say it could be worth putting spending on the card if you’re trying to earn Medallion elite status with Delta SkyMiles. For most people, the reason you’ll want to keep this card long term is because of the perks and benefits that it offers, which for many people will more than offset the annual fee. Let’s go over some of those benefits.

Every year upon renewal of your Delta Platinum Card, you can receive a Delta Main roundtrip companion certificate. You just have to pay the government-imposed taxes and fees for the companion. This is a great deal that can be worth significantly more than the annual fee in and of itself.

If redeeming the certificate there are some things to be aware of:

Just for having the Delta Platinum Card, you can receive up to $150 in Delta Stays credit annually. The way this works, you can receive $150 in statement credits per calendar year when you use your card to pay for a new Delta Stays prepaid hotel or vacation rental booking on the Delta Stays platform.

While I’m not usually a fan of using airline portals to book hotel stays and vacation rentals, this could prove worthwhile, as you can use it for a hotel stay costing right around $150, if you wanted to. If used right, there’s real value here.

Just for having the Delta Platinum Card, you receive up to $120 in rideshare credits annually (Enrollment required). The way this works, you can receive up to $10 in statement credits each month after using your card on U.S. rideshare purchases with select providers. This is super easy to unlock, though admittedly the increments as such are quite small.

Just for having the Delta Platinum Card, you receive up to $120 in Resy credits annually (Enrollment required). The way this works, you can receive up to $10 in statement credits each month after using your card on eligible purchases with U.S. Resy restaurants.

Just for having the Platinum Delta Card you get a first checked bag free. With the ever-increasing cost of a checked bag with Delta, this can really add up.

Depending on how many bags you’re checking, a single trip could pay for the card’s annual fee.

You receive priority boarding just for having the Delta Platinum Amex. This helps maximize your odds of finding space for your carry-on and getting to your seat sooner. To receive this benefit, you’ll need to ensure the primary cardmember’s SkyMiles number is linked to the reservation (though there’s no need to actually pay for the flight with the card).

This benefit is valid for a total of up to nine people traveling on the same reservation with the primary cardmember.

If you have the Delta Platinum Card, then you can save 20% in the form of a statement credit for eligible pre-purchased meals, and in-flight purchases of food, alcoholic beverages, and audio headsets, on Delta flights. Allow 8-12 weeks for the statement credit to post.

The Platinum Delta Amex offers a Global Entry or TSA PreCheck credit. This benefit applies once every four years for the application fee for TSA PreCheck or Global Entry. This can save you time both at security and immigration, and is something I highly recommend signing up for if eligible. (Enrollment required)

Delta has a Pay With Miles feature, where if you have a Delta co-branded credit card, you can redeem miles for one cent each toward a Delta flight purchase (in increments of 5,000 miles per $50). That’s not the best deal in the world, though this is a feature that’s exclusively available to those with an eligible Delta Amex card.

Some people find this to be useful since they can redeem their miles toward flights, and then they still earn miles and MQDs on the portion of the fare they pay in cash.

With the TakeOff 15 perk (exclusively for those with select Delta Amex cards), you can save 15% on the cost of a SkyMiles award ticket when traveling exclusively on Delta (the discount doesn’t apply to taxes and fees). Delta SkyMiles award pricing is dynamic, and generally you’ll find that each mile gets you a bit over a cent toward the cost of a ticket.

Saving 15% on these awards is valuable, and means that you’ll generally get somewhere around 1.2-1.3 cents of value per mile (or sometimes even more). In many cases this will end up being a better value than using the Pay With Miles option, so it’s a real perk of the card.

One of the great features of Amex cards is access to Amex Offers, which offers savings or bonus points on purchases with all kinds of retailers. There’s huge value to be had in getting as many Amex cards as possible, so that you can get these offers on multiple cards.

Amex Offers could save you hundreds of dollars per year. You can access these offers by logging into your account and scrolling down to the bottom of your account summary page. (Enrollment required)

The Delta Platinum Card gets you complimentary Hertz Five Star status. Enrollment is required, and you receive the following benefits with the rental car company:

The Delta Platinum Amex comes with a handful of coverage benefits that can protect you and your belongings both at home and on the road, including:

Up to $300 per Covered Trip that is delayed for more than 12 hours; and 2 claims per Eligible Card per 12 consecutive month period. Eligibility and Benefit level varies by Card. Terms, Conditions, and Limitations Apply. Please visit americanexpress.com/benefitsguide for more details. Underwritten by New Hampshire Insurance Company, an AIG Company. Baggage insurance plan: Eligibility and Benefit level varies by Card. Terms, Conditions, and Limitations Apply. Please visit americanexpress.com/benefitsguide for more details. Underwritten by AMEX Assurance Company. Car rental loss and damage insurance: Eligibility and Benefit level varies by Card. Terms, Conditions, and Limitations Apply. Please visit americanexpress.com/benefitsguide for more details. Underwritten by AMEX Assurance Company. Car Rental Loss or Damage Coverage is offered through American Express Travel Related Services Company, Inc. Extended warranty and purchase protection: Eligibility and Benefit level varies by Card. Terms, Conditions, and Limitations Apply. Please visit americanexpress.com/benefitsguide for more details. Underwritten by AMEX Assurance Company.

The Delta Platinum Credit Card isn’t necessarily the best card for the casual Delta flyer, and it’s also not a card I’d recommend putting much spending on, unless you value the MQDs that you can earn with the card. Even if you value MQDs, you’re better off with the more premium card, since you can earn them twice as fast.

However, this card has solid perks, ranging from a companion certificate, to free checked bags, to priority boarding, to savings on award flights, to access to exclusive award redemption opportunities, to valuable statement credits, and more.

Bigger picture, is the Delta Platinum Card worth it, though? There are a few things to consider.

If the Delta Platinum Amex sounds interesting to you but you are instead looking for a card for your small business, consider the Delta SkyMiles® Platinum Business American Express Card.

Most of the benefits of the card are the same. The main earning difference is that the business card earns 1.5x miles on transit, at U.S. shipping providers, and on single eligible purchases of $5,000 or more (on up to $100,000 of combined eligible purchases per year), while the personal card offers 2x miles at restaurants worldwide and U.S. supermarkets (both cards offer 3x miles on Delta purchases and hotel purchases).

The business version of the card also offers an annual Delta Stays credit of up to $200, rather than one of up to $150, so it’s arguably more lucrative.

The Delta SkyMiles® Gold American Express Card (learn more) is a good card for occasional Delta flyers who want basic airline perks. It has a $0 introductory annual fee for the first year, then $150. (Rates & Fees) and a smaller list of perks, including:

The Delta Gold Card offers the same discounts you get with the Delta Platinum Card, as well as the rideshare credit, but in this case it only kicks in after your first renewal. The Delta Gold Card doesn’t earn MQDs toward status, so that’s another potential downside to keep in mind.

For the very frequent Delta flyer, there’s the Delta SkyMiles® Reserve American Express Card (learn more), which has a $650 annual fee (Rates & Fees). What differentiates this card?

If you are looking to earn Delta SkyMiles through credit card spending then consider using a card earning Amex Membership Rewards points. These points can be transferred to Delta SkyMiles at a 1:1 ratio, and you can in many cases earn points at a much faster rate.

For example, the American Express® Gold Card (learn more) offers 4x points at restaurants worldwide (on up to $50K per calendar year, and then 1x) and at U.S. supermarkets (on up to $25K per calendar year, and then 1x), and 3x points on flights booked directly with airlines or at amextravel.com

Furthermore, earning Amex points gives you more flexibility to redeem in other ways, given all the great uses of Membership Rewards points.

The information and associated card details on this page for the American Express Green Card have been collected independently by OMAAT and have not been reviewed or provided by the card issuer.

The information and associated card details on this page for the American Express Green Card have been collected independently by OMAAT and have not been reviewed or provided by the card issuer.

The Delta Platinum Amex offers solid perks for those who fly Delta frequently, especially Medallion members. For many, the annual companion certificate will more than justify the annual fee in and of itself, without even accounting for all of the other perks. Some will also get value from the 2,500 MQDs that are offered annually just for having the card.

The annual fee on this card is potentially quite easy to justify, thanks to all the credits you can earn with rideshares, Resy, and even Delta Stays.

If you want to learn more about the Delta Platinum Amex Card, follow this link.

#6117. Updated: Frontier Airlines Flight Declares Mayday After Lavatory Floods The Cabin — “We’re Worried About Electronics”

A bathroom sink sprang a leak on Frontier Airlines flight 3566, spraying so much water into the cabin that the pilot declared “Mayday, Mayday, Mayday” and requested a diversion. It was so bad he told air traffic control, “We’re worried about electronics.” The Denver – Detroit flight landed safely in Chicago. This may be the most Frontier Airlines story ever that doesn’t involve a passenger fight. The November 11 flight was operated by an Airbus A321neo N688FR. “Our forward lav sink has sprung a leak and it’s spraying so much water, it’s flooding, uh, the cabin area in the back. #6116. Korean Air Adds Newark Flights From Incheon, Joining United & Air Premia

Korean Air has just quietly added a new long haul route, as the airline will be adding service to Newark, New Jersey. What’s interesting is just how competitive this market has become, but it’s logical in the context of what’s going on at the airline (thanks to S_LEE for flagging this).

As of May 22, 2027, Korean Air plans to launch daily nonstop flights between Seoul Incheon (ICN) and Newark. The flight will operate with the following schedule:

KE97 Seoul Incheon to Newark departing 10:00PM arriving 11:00PMKE98 Newark to Seoul Incheon departing 1:00AM arriving 5:15AM (+1 day)

The 6,896-mile flight is blocked at 14hr to the United States, and 15hr15min to South Korea. Korean Air will use a Boeing 777-300ER for the route, featuring 277 seats, including eight first class seats, 42 business class seats, and 227 economy seats.

This technically marks a service resumption, as Korean Air last served Newark through September 2001, but then suspended flights after the 9/11 terror attacks, and never resumed the flights. This new service will complement Korean Air’s existing service to New York Kennedy (JFK), which typically operates twice daily.

On top of that, Korean Air’s destinations in the United States include Atlanta (ATL), Boston (BOS), Chicago (ORD), Dallas (DFW), Honolulu (HNL), Las Vegas (LAS), Los Angeles (LAX), San Francisco (SFO), Seattle (SEA), and Washington Dulles (IAD).

Interestingly, Korean Air faces quite a bit of competition in the market between Incheon and Newark. Going back several years, it’s a route that no airline served.

However, that has changed in recent times. In May 2023, South Korean budget carrier Air Premia launched service in the market using a Boeing 787. Then in September 2026, United Airlines launched flights in the market, also using a Boeing 787. Korean Air’s timing is very similar to Air Premia’s in both directions, which isn’t too surprising.

Some people might be surprised to see Korean Air adding flights to Newark in addition to existing service to Kennedy (with no plans to reduce that service), but this actually seems pretty straightforward to me.

Keep in mind that Korean Air and Asiana have merged, and in the coming weeks, the two airlines will even take on the same brand. Historically these carriers were huge competitors, so of course in some markets they’ll be reducing capacity. In other words, the combined Korean Air won’t have quite as many frequencies to places like Los Angeles, New York, and San Francisco, as the two airlines did separately.

That of course opens up the opportunity to serve more new markets, and clearly Newark was identified as one of those opportunities. Also keep in mind that Korean Air operates as part of a transpacific joint venture with Delta, so the airlines can coordinate fares and schedules, and it’s all about the combined depth and breadth of service.

If you’re looking at this from a Manhattan centric perspective, you might be surprised that the airline is bothering to serve both airports. However, service to Newark goes way beyond that, and the idea is that this flight is useful for serving parts of New Jersey, Pennsylvania, etc. Admittedly those flyers likely aren’t loyal to SkyTeam, but from a Korea point of sale perspective (especially with the number of people studying in the region), it makes sense.

As of May 2027, Korean Air will be launching daily flights from Seoul Incheon to Newark, complementing existing service to Kennedy. This means we’ll see three daily flights between Incheon and Newark on three different airlines… that’s quite the step up from the zero daily flights we saw several years back!

With Korean Air’s takeover of Asiana complete, it’s logical that the South Korean mega carrier would be looking at adding some new markets, given the increased connectivity and scale of the operation.

What do you make of Korean Air launching Newark flights?

If you typically fly with American Airlines and its partner airlines, earning elite status in the AAdvantage program can unlock many perks, from complimentary upgrades to priority boarding.

In 2022, American AAdvantage revamped the method for earning elite status to a system based on Loyalty Points.

Nowadays, members earn Loyalty Points through eligible flights, credit card spending and purchases with participating partners.

Here’s what you need to know about American Airlines elite status, including how to earn it and what benefits it brings.

American Airlines elite status gives perks to AAdvantage members who interact with the program and its partners. The program lets you earn Loyalty Points toward elite status through many activities unrelated to travel, including shopping, dining and spending on cobranded American Airlines credit cards.

You can earn each American Airlines elite status tier by accumulating a set amount of Loyalty Points during the elite-qualification year that runs for 12 months from March 1 through the end of February. Once you reach the threshold, your status takes effect immediately and remains valid through March 31 of the following full year.

Note: Loyalty Points and AAdvantage miles are not the same thing (but more on that below).

Related: Last-minute strategies for earning American AAdvantage elite status

You’ll find four published tiers of American Airlines elite status that you can earn by accumulating Loyalty Points during the 12 months starting each March 1:

In addition to these tiers, there’s also the exclusive, invite-only Concierge Key status. However, American AAdvantage doesn’t publish any specific requirements for this status.

You’ll also earn Loyalty Point Rewards as you reach specific Loyalty Point thresholds, including some that fall between elite status tiers. You’ll earn your first Loyalty Point Rewards choice after earning 15,000 Loyalty Points within the 12-month qualification period beginning March 1.

Related: Your guide to American Airlines Million Miler status

To qualify for American Airlines elite status, you must earn the required number of Loyalty Points during each 12-month qualification period following March 1. As discussed, you’ll need to earn 40,000 Loyalty Points for Gold status, 75,000 for Platinum, 125,000 for Platinum Pro and 200,000 for Executive Platinum each qualification period.

We have a full guide to earning Loyalty Points. But, in short, you'll earn two types of American Airlines miles: base and bonus. And while both base and bonus miles are redeemable, generally only base miles earn Loyalty Points. The exception is the elite status bonus on flights, which also counts (more on that below). So, each time you earn a base mile with AAdvantage, you'll also earn a Loyalty Point.

You can earn American AAdvantage base miles through many different activities. Here’s a noncomprehensive list of some ways you can earn base miles (and hence Loyalty Points):

There are many other ways to earn American Airlines miles. However, check whether you’re earning base or bonus miles before you get too excited about how many Loyalty Points you’ll earn. Bask Bank mileage accounts are one example of an activity earning only bonus miles — hence, no Loyalty Points. Basic Economy fares on American don't earn Loyalty Points either.

Note: American and Hyatt ended their enhanced loyalty partnership in 2026, so World of Hyatt status is no longer offered as a Loyalty Point Reward. You can still earn 500 AAdvantage miles per eligible Hyatt stay by giving your AAdvantage number at check-in.

Related: Be careful: 9 times you won’t earn American Airlines Loyalty Points, even if you earn miles

American Airlines elite status comes with some valuable benefits. Here’s a look at some of the most noteworthy benefits, including how they differ by status tier.

American Airlines elite members receive complimentary upgrades on eligible flights to select destinations within North America, the Caribbean and Central America, subject to availability. Depending on the aircraft, these upgrades can move members from Main Cabin to premium economy, from Premium Economy to business or domestic first class, or directly from Main Cabin to business or domestic first class (on aircraft without a Premium Economy cabin).

These upgrades are automatically requested and are available on paid tickets and award tickets. Members can also receive a complimentary upgrade for one companion traveling on the same flight. However, Basic Economy tickets purchased on or after May 18, 2026, aren't eligible for complimentary upgrades.

American will start processing these upgrades at different times depending on your American Airlines elite status tier. Executive Platinum members may have their upgrades confirmed as early as 100 hours before departure, Platinum Pro members as early as 72 hours, Platinum members as early as 48 hours and Gold members as early as 24 hours.

American Airlines prioritizes upgrades — including complimentary upgrades, mileage award upgrades and systemwide upgrades — in the following order:

Members with American Airlines elite status — and up to eight passengers traveling with you on the same reservation — can select Preferred seats without any extra fees during booking or anytime after booking (based on availability). Preferred seats have standard legroom but are located in more desirable locations throughout the economy cabin. This benefit does not apply to Basic Economy tickets purchased on or after May 18, 2026.

Main Cabin Extra seats, which offer additional legroom, are also complimentary for AAdvantage elite members and up to eight companions traveling on the same reservation (based on availability). Executive Platinum, Platinum Pro and Platinum members can select these seats at booking, while Gold members must wait until within 24 hours of departure. Basic Economy tickets purchased on or after May 18, 2026, are not eligible for complimentary Main Cabin Extra seats.

American Airlines elite members get a mileage bonus as follows when flying on eligible flights:

The status bonus is added to the base miles earned on eligible flights, and unlike most bonus miles, it counts toward Loyalty Points as well. For example, on flights marketed by American, a member without status earns 5 miles and Loyalty Points per dollar, while an Executive Platinum member earns 11. That makes it easier for higher-tier members to requalify through flying.

AAdvantage elite members enjoy priority access at check-in, security and boarding on eligible American Airlines flights. Specifically, Executive Platinum members board in Group 1, Platinum Pro in Group 2, Platinum in Group 3 and Gold in Group 4. Boarding with any of these groups might mean there’s still space in the overhead bin for your carry-on suitcase.

AAdvantage status members also get priority when standing by for a different American Airlines flight on the same day of travel (and can standby for a later flight the same day) on eligible flights within the U.S. and between the U.S., Puerto Rico and the U.S. Virgin Islands.

Executive Platinum and Platinum Pro members — and up to eight companions traveling with them on the same reservation — can enjoy complimentary same-day confirmed flight changes on American when flying to or from the U.S., Puerto Rico and the U.S. Virgin Islands.

AAdvantage elite members also enjoy complimentary checked bags when flying American Airlines: Gold members get their first checked bag free, Platinum members get their first two checked bags free, and Platinum Pro and Executive Platinum members get their first three checked bags free. Best of all, this checked baggage allowance is also offered to guests traveling with the status member on the same reservation.

American Airlines elite status offers a variety of other perks, including the following:

Finally, American Airlines offers additional rewards at specific Loyalty Point milestones. Though these rewards are separate from AAdvantage elite status, you’ll inherently unlock them as you accumulate Loyalty Points toward the program's elite status tiers.

Here’s a look at the Loyalty Point Rewards you could choose as you progress toward the 200,000 Loyalty Points required for Executive Platinum status:

Related: Why (and how) I'm earning AAdvantage Platinum Pro elite status and not going for AAdvantage Executive Platinum

Having a cobranded American Airlines credit card is extremely helpful if you want to earn American Airlines elite status. Although the sign-up and category bonuses provide bonus miles — which won’t give you Loyalty Points — you’ll earn 1 Loyalty Point per dollar spent with all U.S.-issued AAdvantage credit cards. This means you can boost your Loyalty Point balance as you use your card for purchases and even qualify for American elite status from credit card spending alone.

If you value Admirals Club access, the (see rates and fees) is an excellent choice. Meanwhile, existing cardholders who had the AAdvantage® Aviator® World Elite Silver Mastercard® and were transitioned to the (see rates and fees) can still earn up to 15,000 additional Loyalty Points by meeting specific spending thresholds during the qualification year ending Feb. 28, 2027. Unfortunately, this benefit is not available to new Globe card applicants.

The information for the Aviator Silver card has been collected independently by The Points Guy. The card details on this page have not been reviewed or provided by the card issuer.

American Airlines elite status is worth it for some travelers. I've held Platinum Pro or Executive Platinum status since 2016 because I value the domestic upgrades, waived checked bag fees, Priority check-in lines and Oneworld Emerald status these tiers provide.

But, after reconsidering what I value in American Airlines elite status, I've only strived to qualify for Platinum Pro in recent years. In short, I decided the incremental value of Executive Platinum over Platinum Pro didn’t justify the extra costs I’d incur to earn the higher status.

It’s important to consider how much you’ll use your AAdvantage perks and the cost of earning American Airlines status. If you’ll organically earn American Airlines status through flights, then it’s likely worth earning. But if you’ll have to earn a significant number of Loyalty Points through other means, such as using the AAdvantage eShopping portal or spending on an AAdvantage credit card, there’s an opportunity cost to doing so.

Finally, if you’ll only use your American Airlines elite status perks occasionally or only need a specific perk, consider whether you can get what you seek through booking premium-cabin fares or applying for a credit card that offers that particular benefit.

Related: Which credit card should you use for American Airlines flights?

American Airlines offers four elite status tiers you can earn by accumulating Loyalty Points: Gold, Platinum, Platinum Pro and Executive Platinum. These tiers offer perks including Preferred seats, complimentary space-available upgrades on eligible American Airlines flights, and Oneworld perks on select partner airlines.

If you frequently fly with American Airlines, British Airways or Iberia on expensive paid fares or spend a significant amount on American Airlines credit cards or when shopping through the AAdvantage eShopping portal, you’ll likely find it easy and worthwhile to earn American Airlines elite status. Otherwise, it's smart to consider whether the value you'll get from American Airlines status is worth the cost you'll incur to earn it.

#6113. America Needs an Arsenal of Democracies

We must combine American and allied innovation and manufacturing to take on the threats we share.

A worker along the assembly line handles large caliber 155mm metal projectiles at the Scranton Army Ammunition Plant in Scranton, Pa., April 16, 2024.

An Israeli-developed missile is now rolling off an American production line. On October 9, Raytheon-Rafael Protection Systems, an American Israeli joint venture, announced the first Tamir interceptors manufactured in Camden, Ark. They are intended for Israel’s Iron Dome missile-defense system, with plans to produce a U.S. variant for the Marine Corps.

The Camden facility builds on decades of allied weapons production, including the AIM-9 Sidewinder air-to-air missile with West Germany as well as the F-16 with multiple partners. But today’s conflicts require an industrial network that produces weapons at scale, maintains deliveries during disruptions, and replenishes forces across theaters. Co-production alone does not deliver that. It changes where a weapon is built; resilience depends on whether production can continue when something breaks.

#6112. Scoop: Frontier Airlines Plans First Class Service—Not Just Bigger Seats

Frontier Airlines is planning more than a bigger seat for first class. A new memo tells flight attendants that first class service standards are coming for flights beginning March 5, 2027, the same day its new front cabin launches. This follows my original scoop, since confirmed by the airline, that Frontier’s first class rolls out March 5, 2027. Under “Onboard service,” the airline now says: Our standard onboard services apply through March 4, 2027. New First Class service standards will be released for flights on and after March 5, 2027. This is a move toward a real first class service, and away from the Spirit Airlines ‘Big Front Seat’ approach to just selling more space. This hasn’t been announced publicly yet. The airline’s first class frequently asked questions, updated just yesterday, still says food and beverages are available for purchase. Specific standards are still to come. Frontier Has Confirmed The March 5 Launch Frontier originally announced first class in December 2024 for late 2025. Last month I reported that aircraft conversions were beginning, with the bigger seats sold as UpFront Plus during the transition. So getting the seat before the March 5 official launch doesn’t mean getting new service with it. Frontier publicly announced first class reservations on November 10, confirming March 5 travel and targeting that date for completion of the seating conversion: Eight first class seats: two rows in a 2-by-2 configuration, with up to 37 inches of pitch. More extra legroom: rows three through eight will offer up to 34 inches of pitch. UpFront Plus, with its blocked middle seat, continues in select rows. A First bundle advertised from $129 one way: first class seating, a carry-on, two checked bags and priority boarding. A Premium bundle advertised from $90 one way: extra legroom seating, a carry-on and priority boarding. The introductory offer requires buying the flight and bundle together by November 16, for select nonstop domestic departures March 5–April 5, 2027. And these seats still don’t recline. Frontier describes them as “pre-reclined,” which means you can’t adjust the seatback. Power And Wi-Fi Are Coming Frontier now says USB-C charging will be offered in the first eight rows, not throughout the full coach cabin. Both power and Starlink wi-fi will roll out during 2027. Frontier’s new renderings show the charging setup: I’ve said that the lack of inflight internet has kept me from flying Frontier. Giving up hours of work can make the cheapest ticket actually more expensive. A bigger seat, power and working wi-fi make a big difference in my willingness to buy travel from them. Their operational reliability, however, is still a caution. Including drinks and food makes sense as it tries to have a product customers interested in a better experience will buy. They’ve had largely the cheap offerings but not the revenue opportunities from further upsells. It’s still not clear what the service standards will mean or translate into in the cabin. Unfortunately, for bookings made starting January 1, 2027, elite frequent flyers will only be eligible for complimentary upgrades to first class if they buy a bundle. And top tier Diamonds only qualify 24 hours prior to departure (18 for Platinum, 8 for Gold, and 4 for Silver). And top tier Diamonds only qualify 24 hours prior to departure (18 for Platinum, 8 for Gold, and 4 for Silver). Frontier originally announced first class in December 2024 for late 2025. Last month I reported that aircraft conversions were beginning, with the bigger seats sold as UpFront Plus during the transition. So getting the seat before the March 5 official launch doesn’t mean getting new service with it.

Frontier publicly announced first class reservations on November 10, confirming March 5 travel and targeting that date for completion of the seating conversion:

The introductory offer requires buying the flight and bundle together by November 16, for select nonstop domestic departures March 5–April 5, 2027.

And these seats still don’t recline. Frontier describes them as “pre-reclined,” which means you can’t adjust the seatback.

Frontier now says USB-C charging will be offered in the first eight rows, not throughout the full coach cabin. Both power and Starlink wi-fi will roll out during 2027. Frontier’s new renderings show the charging setup: I’ve said that the lack of inflight internet has kept me from flying Frontier. Giving up hours of work can make the cheapest ticket actually more expensive. A bigger seat, power and working wi-fi make a big difference in my willingness to buy travel from them. Their operational reliability, however, is still a caution. Including drinks and food makes sense as it tries to have a product customers interested in a better experience will buy. They’ve had largely the cheap offerings but not the revenue opportunities from further upsells. It’s still not clear what the service standards will mean or translate into in the cabin. Unfortunately, for bookings made starting January 1, 2027, elite frequent flyers will only be eligible for complimentary upgrades to first class if they buy a bundle. And top tier Diamonds only qualify 24 hours prior to departure (18 for Platinum, 8 for Gold, and 4 for Silver). #6110. 6 Reasons Why Citi Strata Elite Beats Amex Platinum And Sapphire Reserve

I receive compensation for content and many links on this blog. Be aware that websites may earn compensation when a customer clicks on a link, when an application is approved, or when an account is opened. Citibank is an advertising partner of this site, as is American Express, Chase, Capital One, and others. Any opinions expressed in this post are my own, and have not been reviewed, approved, or endorsed by my advertising partners. I do not write about all offers that are available -- instead focusing on miles, points, and cash back (and currencies that can be converted into the same). Terms apply to the offers and benefits listed on this page.

Citi Strata Elite earns 50% more points on unbonused spending than Amex Platinum or Chase Sapphire Reserve, and those points can become American Airlines miles. It also costs $200 – $300 less per year.

I’ve written a lot about the card’s enormous first-year value. But the more I’ve used the hotel benefit, the more I think there’s a case for the Citi Strata EliteSM Card (See rates and fees) beyond the initial bonus. Here are six things it does better than Amex Platinum and Sapphire Reserve – both excellent cards and I have them both.

Banks advertise how many transfer partners they have. A long list can include many I even actively avoid (Aeromexico, Thai Airways). Most banks are also limited in whom they can work with because major airline and hotel cobrand card agreements usually include exclusivity provisions that limit what competing banks can offer. American Express has Delta. Chase has United. Citi has American. Of those three, I’d take American AAdvantage. Strata Elite points transfer to American at 1:1. And American still offers some terrific partner redemptions. However, some of my best American redemptions are just regular domestic coach trips. I’ve written about getting 4 cents and even 8 cents per mile from economy awards. American will sometimes make a flight cheap in miles while keeping the cash fare high. You don’t need to want a first class suite halfway around the world to get value from this program. Citi still has international partners I want, including Air France KLM Flying Blue, Singapore Airlines and Qatar Airways. Chase’s Hyatt transfers are a real advantage on the hotel side. (I still wish Bank of America had its own transferable points program, with Alaska’s Atmos Rewards as a partner.) 2. The Hotel Credit Works Beyond A Short List Of Luxury Properties Strata Elite offers up to $300 off prepaid hotel stays of two nights or longer booked through Citi Travel each calendar year. The discount comes off when you book, and applies to the room cost before taxes and fees. You can use it at ordinary hotels and independent properties, without restricting yourself to a luxury collection. Amex Platinum’s $600 annual hotel credit is split into two $300 periods and requires Fine Hotels + Resorts or The Hotel Collection bookings. Sapphire Reserve’s $500 The Edit credit is limited to that collection, with a maximum of $250 per qualifying booking. Chase also has an additional 2026 hotel credit, but that one is restricted to selected brands. Those programs can provide real value through breakfast, property credits and hotel loyalty benefits. Citi’s advantage is the much broader choice of hotels where I can use the discount. And I haven’t found that using Citi’s credit requires giving back the savings through a higher room rate. In January, I compared the Marriott at LaGuardia Airport: Citi Travel was $156 before taxes, while Marriott’s own member rate was $176. That’s $20 less per night before applying the credit. I still compare the room and cancellation terms, but Citi Travel has been competitive or even cheaper. I’ve also had little difficulty getting Marriott hotels to add my Bonvoy number at check-in and honor on-property benefits. Earlier this year I used the Strata Elite credit at a Marriott and received club lounge access. I similarly had no problem getting status recognition on a bank portal booking at a Westin this month. These third-party bookings generally aren’t supposed to be eligible for hotel points, elite-night credit or elite benefits. 3. It’s A Better Card For Everyday Spending Strata Elite earns 1.5 points per dollar on spending outside its bonus categories. Sapphire Reserve and Amex Platinum earn just one. You can do better with any bank pairing its primary card with a second card that offers different earn. Generally you’re permitted to pool those points. 4. Six Points Per Dollar On Weekend Evening Dining Is Fantastic Citi Nights earns six points per dollar at restaurants from 6 p.m. Friday until 6 a.m. Saturday, and again from 6 p.m. Saturday until 6 a.m. Sunday, all times Eastern. This works at restaurants generally, including qualifying restaurant delivery services. You don’t have to pick from a bank’s restaurant reservation list. Citi uses the time the purchase is authorized, so a Friday dinner doesn’t lose the bonus just because the charge posts on Monday. Outside Citi Nights, restaurant spending earns 3x. And Citi’s other big accelerators are 12x on hotels, car rentals and attractions booked through Citi Travel, and 6x on airfare booked there. You don’t earn points on the hotel spending covered by the $300 benefit. For airfare booked directly with an airline, Amex Platinum’s 5x and Sapphire Reserve’s 4x beat Citi’s 1.5x. Big Useful Credits Instead Of Many Small Ones I’ve laid out how to use the Strata Elite credits, but the basic approach is pretty simple: book a hotel stay and buy an American Airlines ticket. In addition to the $300 hotel benefit, there’s a $200 annual Splurge credit. Select American Airlines as one of your eligible merchants before purchasing, and a ticket billed directly by American qualifies. You don’t have to find incidental fees to use it on, as with Amex Platinum’s airline fee credit. The other choices are Best Buy, 1stDibs, Live Nation and Future Personal Training. You can activate up to two merchants at a time and use the credit over multiple eligible purchases. For me, American makes this easy. If the hotel benefit and Splurge credit replace $500 you’d have spent anyway, they leave just $95 of Citi’s $595 annual fee to cover. And both benefits run by calendar year, without dividing the money into monthly allowances. There’s also up to $200 a year for Blacklane, divided into $100 for January through June and $100 for July through December. 6. The Annual Fee Is Lower The annual fees are $595 for Citi Strata Elite vs $795 for Sapphire Reserve and $895 for Amex Platinum. You still get a premium travel card: Priority Pass lounge access with up to two guests, four Admirals Club passes each calendar year for eligible American or oneworld travel, travel protections, and up to $120 for a Global Entry or TSA PreCheck application every four years. And the first year still offers a lot. The current offer is 75,000 bonus points after spending $6,000 in the first three months. At 1.5 cents apiece, that’s $1,125 in points before counting what you earn from the spending itself. Someone opening the card now can use the hotel and Splurge benefits during the rest of 2026 and again in 2027, before their first anniversary. That’s up to $1,000 from those two benefits alone. If those credits replace spending you’d make anyway, the bonus plus the credits less the $595 fee comes to $1,530 in first-year value, before Blacklane, lounge access or points earned from purchases. The annual fees are $595 for Citi Strata Elite vs $795 for Sapphire Reserve and $895 for Amex Platinum. You still get a premium travel card: Priority Pass lounge access with up to two guests, four Admirals Club passes each calendar year for eligible American or oneworld travel, travel protections, and up to $120 for a Global Entry or TSA PreCheck application every four years. And the first year still offers a lot. The current offer is 75,000 bonus points after spending $6,000 in the first three months. At 1.5 cents apiece, that’s $1,125 in points before counting what you earn from the spending itself. Someone opening the card now can use the hotel and Splurge benefits during the rest of 2026 and again in 2027, before their first anniversary. That’s up to $1,000 from those two benefits alone. If those credits replace spending you’d make anyway, the bonus plus the credits less the $595 fee comes to $1,530 in first-year value, before Blacklane, lounge access or points earned from purchases. #6109. Why Russia Is Targeting European Freezers

Rearmament isn’t just for the battlefield — civil defense matters, too.

A woman walks past partially empty shelves at a SuperValu store in Blanchardstown, Dublin, Ireland, November 2, 2026.

Twice in the space of a few weeks, Russian hackers have managed to seize control of supermarket refrigeration systems in Europe. It began with hundreds of French stores in mid-October, after which, in early November, hackers struck outlets in Sweden, Belgium, Ireland, the Netherlands, and elsewhere. The hackers remotely forced freezers and chillers into prolonged defrost mode, driving temperatures to more than 120 degrees Fahrenheit and spoiling large quantities of food. These attacks have revealed an underrated aspect of rearmament that has so far been almost completely overlooked: civil defense.

Hackers behind most ransomware attacks demand payment. These hackers simply disrupted Europe’s food supply and left without a message. Only a few days after the most recent (as of this writing) attacks, in early November, did a Russian group finally claim responsibility. European policymakers who may have wished that some random teenagers were behind the attacks instead had their fears confirmed: This was a Russian attack against Europe’s food supply.

John Gustavsson is a writer from Sweden and holds a doctorate in economics. He is Senior Editor of Nation & Citizenship at Restoring the West and a former adviser to the Sweden Democrats in the European Parliament.

#6103. “The sitting president doesn’t win”: Ahead of midterms, Trump reflects on himself

On the last day before the 2026 midterm elections, President Donald Trump gave a speech before the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool, a site of considerable scandal in his second term. He joked it should be renamed after him and spent considerable time discussing Washington, D.C. construction projects and resurrecting conspiracy theories about monument vandals. When the president did turn to the elections, more than 23 minutes into an hour-long speech, he seemed to foreshadow major Republican losses in the House and Senate, describing it as “The most important midterm, I believe, in our lifetime.”

“When you vote, remember a party that hates America cannot be allowed to rule over the people who built our country,” Trump said, referring to Democrats, whom he said want to “blow all of this up by electing communist jihadists.”

“If the people that voted for me and voted in the last election where we had such a great victory, if they go out and vote, just a good portion of them, we will win in a landslide,” Trump said midway in his speech. “Now that doesn’t happen because usually whoever the sitting president is, Republican or Democrat, uh, good or bad, good president, great president, bad, for some reason the sitting president doesn’t win the midterms, but we gave this a very strong shot.”

The last day of polling indicates that Democrats have odds that are better than good to flip control of the House and Senate. The final results from the New York Times/Siena University polls report “The party is ahead in all seven states likeliest to decide control of the Senate: Michigan, Kansas, Texas, Maine, Ohio and, more narrowly, Alaska and Iowa.” The final predictions in the Cook Political Report included five additional shifts for Democrats in North Carolina, Florida, Tennessee and Virginia, projecting “that Democrats will win 15 to 25 seats, putting them at a 230- to 240-seat majority.” If a sweep happens in the toss up races, it’ll give Democrats their strongest majority since 2009.

Meanwhile, early voting records have been smashed around the country, in places like South Carolina and Ohio. In Texas, more than 7.7 million voters did so early, surpassing the record turnout for a midterm election set in 2018. Across the nation, about 50 million ballots have already been cast so far, with the share of registered Democrats notably increased in several key state races. But according to the New York Times, around half the expected votes will come on Election Day itself, making it difficult at this point to determine how big a role early votes will play in the outcome.
